stories.title: Alex Albon says Williams is 'fighting fires' all season, worries the team has gone backwards
stories.what_happened: Speaking during F1's summer shutdown, Alex Albon detailed the scale of Williams's struggles through the 2026 season, describing the year as **"very psychological"** because "there is no easy thing… we're also fighting extinguishers. We have little fires that we're trying to put out." Albon said it has been hard to tell what's down to the driver versus what's down to the car, and separately admitted concern that Williams may have gone **"two or three years backwards"** technically this season. The team has now failed to score points in its last five Grands Prix and sits 9th in the constructors' championship heading into the summer break — a marked step down from the progress it had shown in prior seasons. The comments came shortly after Albon reached his 100th race for Williams at the Hungarian Grand Prix in July, making him the team's most-capped driver ever, surpassing Nigel Mansell.
key_points: Alex Albon says Williams's 2026 season has felt like constantly **'putting out little fires'** rather than steady progress.
He's voiced concern the team may have gone **'two or three years backwards'** technically this season.
Williams has **failed to score in its last five Grands Prix** and sits **9th in the constructors' championship** at the summer break.
Albon reached his **100th race with Williams** at the Hungarian GP in July, becoming the team's most-capped driver, eclipsing Nigel Mansell.
He says the team's difficulties are largely **psychological**, making it hard to separate driver form from car performance.

depth.background: Williams is one of F1's most storied teams, with multiple championships in the 1980s and 90s, but spent much of the 2010s and early 2020s near the back of the grid. Under new ownership and management in recent seasons, the team had shown signs of recovery and climbing the order — which makes a slide back to 9th in the constructors' standings this year a notable setback. Albon, who joined Williams in 2022 after stints at Red Bull and Toro Rosso, has been widely seen as extracting more from the car than its raw pace suggests, making his own read on the team's struggles a credible internal signal rather than just an excuse.

stories.title: Afghanistan chase a series-clinching win over Ireland in today's 3rd ODI at Belfast, with World Cup qualification points on the line
stories.what_happened: Afghanistan lead their five-match ODI series against Ireland **1–0** heading into today's third match at the Civil Service Cricket Club in Stormont, Belfast, which began at **9:45am local time**. The series opener on August 5 was **abandoned due to rain**, denying Ireland a chance to bank direct World Cup qualification points from that fixture. Afghanistan then won the second ODI on August 7 by a commanding **92 runs**, posting 299/8 before bowling Ireland out for 207, with opener **Ibrahim Zadran's 84** anchoring the innings (that match also featured Rashid Khan's six-wicket haul). Two further matches remain on **August 12 and 14** to complete the series, meaning today's result could move Afghanistan close to sealing the series outright.
key_points: Afghanistan lead the five-match ODI series **1–0**, with the **3rd ODI** underway today in Belfast.
The series opener was **washed out**, costing Ireland a shot at direct World Cup qualification points.
Afghanistan won the 2nd ODI by **92 runs** (299/8 to 207), built on **Ibrahim Zadran's 84**.
Today's match is at the **Civil Service Cricket Club, Stormont**, starting **9:45am local time**.
Two more ODIs follow on **August 12 and 14** to complete the series.

depth.background: Afghanistan and Ireland are two of the sport's rising associate-turned-full-member nations, and their bilateral series carry real weight because **ODI results feed into qualification points** for global events like the 50-over World Cup — meaning a washed-out or lost match isn't just a missed game, it can cost a team a path to the next World Cup. Afghanistan have built one of the most dangerous white-ball attacks in the world in recent years, anchored by spinner **Rashid Khan**, while Ireland have been trying to use home series like this one to bank qualification points after years of near-misses at cricket's top table.

stories.title: Molbio Diagnostics opens its ₹940-crore IPO today, part of a mega week for India's IPO market
stories.what_happened: Molbio Diagnostics' initial public offering opened for subscription today, August 10, and will remain open through August 12, with a price band set between **₹768 and ₹807 per share**. The **₹940 crore** offering includes a ₹200 crore fresh issue — money that goes directly to the company — and a ₹739.7 crore offer-for-sale, where existing shareholders cash out part of their stake. The minimum retail investment is about ₹14,526 for a lot of 18 shares. Molbio's listing is one of **nine IPOs collectively worth close to ₹7,700 crore** opening this week, alongside firms like Dhoot Transmission, Milky Mist Dairy Food, e-commerce platform Shiprocket, and Behari Lal Engineering — making it one of the most crowded IPO weeks of 2026 for Indian markets. Allotment is expected around August 13, with listing tentatively scheduled for August 17.
key_points: Molbio Diagnostics' IPO opens today, **August 10**, and closes August 12, priced at **₹768–₹807 per share**.
The issue is worth **₹940 crore** — split between a **₹200 crore fresh issue** and a **₹739.7 crore offer-for-sale** by existing shareholders.
It's one of **nine IPOs worth ~₹7,700 crore** launching this week alone, one of India's busiest IPO weeks of the year.
Molbio makes point-of-care **molecular diagnostics** devices — the kind of rapid testing kit used for diseases like TB and COVID-19.
Listing is tentatively set for **August 17** on both the NSE and BSE.

depth.background: Molbio Diagnostics is an Indian molecular diagnostics company known for its **Truenat** platform — portable, battery-operated devices that can run PCR-style tests (the same lab technique used for COVID-19 testing) outside a traditional lab, including in rural clinics. India's IPO market has been unusually active through 2026, with strong retail and institutional demand pulling more companies to list, especially in healthcare, diagnostics, and consumer sectors where India's growing middle class is expanding the customer base. A fresh issue means the company raises new money for itself, while an offer-for-sale lets existing investors (like early-stage backers) sell some of their shares to the public.

stories.title: Ukrainian drones knock out Russia's biggest petrochemical plant, cutting 40% of its LPG supply
stories.what_happened: Drones struck the ZapSibNeftekhim petrochemical complex in Tobolsk, in Russia's Tyumen region, on the afternoon of **August 10**, according to Reuters, which cited three industry sources. The facility was shut down **indefinitely** while the extent of the damage is assessed. Tobolsk normally sells around **4,000 metric tons a day** of a propane-butane mix on Russia's domestic commodity exchange (SPIMEX) — on the first trading day after the strike, **zero volumes** were offered from that loading point. Industry estimates put the plant's annual output at roughly **6 million tonnes of LPG**, about **40% of Russia's total** liquefied-gas production. The plant is a joint effort of Russian energy major SIBUR and sits deep in Siberia, illustrating how far Ukrainian drones can now reach.
key_points: Drones hit **ZapSibNeftekhim** in Tobolsk, Siberia — Russia's **largest petrochemical complex** — on the afternoon of August 10.
The plant makes about **6 million tonnes of LPG a year**, roughly **40% of all of Russia's** liquefied-gas output.
It has been shut down **indefinitely** while Russian operators assess the damage, Reuters sources say.
No liquefied-gas cargoes from Tobolsk were offered on Russia's commodity exchange the next trading day — a sign the halt is real.
It's the latest in a run of **Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure** deep inside the country, far from the front line.

depth.background: **LPG (liquefied petroleum gas)** is the propane-butane mix used for cooking gas, heating, and as a feedstock to make plastics — it's a big export earner for Russia. ZapSibNeftekhim, built by the state-linked petrochemical giant SIBUR, is Russia's flagship facility for turning gas into these products. Since 2025, Ukraine has increasingly used long-range drones to hit oil refineries and gas plants thousands of kilometers from the border, arguing that energy exports fund Russia's war. Russia has suffered repeated fuel shortages at home as a result.

stories.title: Canada races to strike a deal with Trump before a 50% tariff hits $20 billion of its exports on August 19
stories.what_happened: Trump's proclamation sets an additional **50% tariff** on a wide range of Canadian goods — far beyond alcohol, dairy and autos, stretching to wood products, chemicals, minerals, food and textiles — covering close to **$20 billion** in annual trade. It takes effect at one minute past midnight Eastern time on **August 19**. Canadian and US trade officials have been meeting in Washington, including in-person talks between top negotiators, and have agreed to **daily contact** at various levels until the deadline. Canada is reportedly prepared to end its provincial bans on American alcohol brands — a long-standing US complaint — in exchange for relief, and negotiators have revived an old proposal for Canada to accept **quotas** on how much steel and aluminum it ships to the US in return for lower tariffs on those metals. PM Mark Carney says talks now cover 'all strategic sectors,' including autos, but cautioned any deal still needs sign-off 'in the Oval Office.'
key_points: A new **50% US tariff** on roughly **$20 billion** of Canadian goods is due to hit at **12:01am on August 19**.
Trump invoked **Section 338**, a **1930s law never used this way before**, bypassing the normal tariff process.
The tariff applies even to goods that qualify under **USMCA**, the existing North America free-trade pact.
Canada is weighing **ending its bans on US alcohol sales** and a **steel/aluminum export-quota deal** to win relief.
Negotiators are holding **daily meetings** in Washington as the deadline approaches, PM **Mark Carney** says.

depth.background: The US and Canada have been locked in an on-and-off trade fight for much of 2026, with Washington accusing Canada of unfairly favoring its own producers over American alcohol, dairy and auto exports. In July, President Trump signed proclamations invoking **Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930** — a rarely-used, decades-old law that lets a president slap tariffs of up to 50% on a country found to discriminate against US commerce. It has never been used this way in the modern tariff era. The **USMCA** (the US-Mexico-Canada trade deal that replaced NAFTA) was supposed to guarantee tariff-free trade on qualifying goods, but these new tariffs apply regardless.

stories.title: Asian markets jump to record highs as a weak US jobs report fuels bets on a Fed rate cut
stories.what_happened: On Monday, August 10, Japan's **Nikkei 225 rose roughly 2%** to a new record high, South Korea's KOSPI added **1.1%**, and the broader MSCI Asia-Pacific index (excluding Japan) gained 0.8%, as the region extended a rally that began on Wall Street on Friday. The trigger was Friday's US jobs report, which showed the world's largest economy **lost 23,000 jobs in July** instead of adding the roughly 85,000 economists expected, pushing unemployment up to 4.1%. Futures markets responded by sharply cutting the odds of a Fed rate hike and raising the odds the central bank instead holds steady or cuts. **China moved against the regional grain**: its CSI 300 index fell 0.4% after inflation data reinforced concerns about sluggish domestic demand. Meanwhile the dollar held near **158.2 yen**, still under pressure days after Japan and the US carried out a rare joint currency intervention to prop up the yen.
key_points: Japan's **Nikkei 225 jumped about 2%** to a fresh record high on Monday.
South Korea's **KOSPI rose 1.1%**, extending Wall Street's Friday rally into Asia.
The US economy actually **lost 23,000 jobs in July**, versus forecasts for +85,000 — a rare, alarming miss.
**China's CSI 300 fell 0.4%**, moving against the regional trend on weak domestic demand data.
The **yen stayed near 158.2/dollar**, still fragile after last week's rare joint Japan-US intervention.

depth.background: The US Federal Reserve sets America's benchmark interest rate to balance inflation against employment. When the US economy looks weaker than expected, traders often bet the Fed will hold off on raising rates — or even cut them — to support growth, and cheaper expected borrowing costs tend to lift stock markets worldwide because it makes future company profits more valuable today. Going into Friday, Fed officials were actually split, with some favoring a rate **hike** as soon as September if inflation stayed sticky.

stories.title: Jharkhand student protesters march on the Assembly as Congress chief Kharge pledges support
stories.what_happened: Hundreds of students, many of them JPSC/JSSC exam aspirants, held a 'Vidhan Sabha Gherao' — a march aimed at surrounding the state Assembly — in Ranchi today, prompting Jharkhand police to tighten security and impose prohibitory orders across the city. The protest has now run for over two weeks with **six rounds of talks** between students and the state government failing to resolve the dispute. Congress president **Mallikarjun Kharge** said the party stands with the students 'irrespective of whether the government concerned is led by an ally or a political rival,' pledging to write to the government and raise the issue. Separately, the Congress's Jharkhand in-charge met Chief Minister Hemant Soren and submitted a memorandum of the students' demands.
key_points: Students staged a **'Vidhan Sabha Gherao'** march on Jharkhand's state Assembly in Ranchi today.
Security was **tightened across Ranchi** ahead of the march, now in its 16th-day-plus phase.
Congress president **Mallikarjun Kharge** publicly pledged the party's support to the protesters.
The protest is over alleged **irregularities in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams**.
Several student leaders remain on an **indefinite hunger strike**, with one's blood glucose reported critically low.

depth.background: For over two weeks, students aspiring to join the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) — the state's main recruitment exam bodies — have been protesting alleged malpractice and irregularities in those exams. Several rounds of talks with the state government led by Chief Minister Hemant Soren have failed to produce a breakthrough, with student leaders demanding a CID probe into the exam bodies and cancellation of a disputed civil-services exam. A handful of protest leaders have been on hunger strike for roughly a week, with one's health deteriorating.

thread.previously: The protest had reached a sixth round of talks with the state government, with no breakthrough on students' demands.
thread.changed: Students escalated with an Assembly march today as security was tightened in Ranchi, and Congress president Kharge publicly pledged the party's support.

stories.title: Adrian Newey's Aston Martin chassis turnaround shifts the pressure onto Honda's engine
stories.what_happened: Aston Martin brought a major **16-part upgrade package** to the Hungarian Grand Prix that overhauled the car in almost every area except its engine, gearbox, and front suspension. The changes roughly **halved the team's pace deficit** to the front of the field overnight, allowing Fernando Alonso to make it out of Q1 qualifying for the first time in a while. The turnaround is being credited to Newey's design leadership after a torrid start to the season, when the team's Honda-powered car suffered vibrations so severe that Newey said in Melbourne his drivers could not finish races. With the chassis now dramatically improved, the remaining performance gap is increasingly being pinned on **Honda's power unit**, putting pressure on the engine manufacturer to deliver further gains.
key_points: A **16-part upgrade package** at the Hungarian Grand Prix roughly **halved** Aston Martin's pace deficit overnight.
Design chief **Adrian Newey** had said in Melbourne the car's Honda power unit vibrated so badly drivers couldn't finish races.
Aston Martin had been stuck **10th of 11 teams**, ahead of only new entrant Cadillac, before the Hungary upgrades.
Fernando Alonso made it out of **Q1** for the first time in a while after the new parts arrived.
With the chassis now competitive, attention turns to whether **Honda's engine** can keep pace for the rest of 2026.

depth.background: Aston Martin hired legendary designer Adrian Newey — architect of championship-winning cars at Williams, McLaren, and Red Bull — to lead its push toward the front of the F1 grid, pairing him with a new-for-2026 partnership with Honda as engine supplier. The team's 2026 season started disastrously: the new car, built for F1's overhauled 2026 technical rules, was several seconds off the pace with a Honda power unit suffering severe vibration issues, leaving the team stuck near the back of an 11-team grid that now includes new entrant Cadillac.

stories.title: Mainland Europe's first total solar eclipse since 1999 sweeps across Spain tomorrow
stories.what_happened: A total solar eclipse will track across eastern Greenland, western Iceland, and the northern half of Spain and northeast Portugal on **August 12, 2026**, with skywatchers across Europe already making travel plans. In Spain, totality begins at roughly **18:27 GMT** in the west and lasts up to **110 seconds**, occurring as a 'golden hour' eclipse just before sunset with the Sun low in the sky. The path of totality crosses Spain west to east through provincial capitals including **Oviedo, León, Bilbao, Zaragoza and Valencia**, putting an estimated **15 million people** directly in its path. Elsewhere in Europe, including the UK and Ireland, the Sun will only be partially obscured, with more than **90%** coverage visible in many places.
key_points: A **total solar eclipse** crosses Spain and Portugal on **August 12**, the first over mainland Europe since **1999**.
Totality lasts up to **2 minutes 18 seconds** at its longest, over Iceland and Greenland.
Roughly **15 million people**, mostly in Spain, live inside the path of totality.
Major cities including **Bilbao, Zaragoza and Valencia** all fall inside the path.
In the UK and Ireland, viewers will see a **partial eclipse**, with over **90% of the Sun** obscured.

depth.background: A total solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun, fully blocking sunlight for a narrow band of the planet below — the 'path of totality' — while nearby regions see only a partial eclipse. Because the Moon's shadow only touches a thin strip of Earth's surface each time, any given location waits decades between total eclipses; mainland Europe's last one was in **1999**. This one first touches land in eastern Greenland and western Iceland before sweeping over northern Spain and the northeast tip of Portugal.

stories.title: Fernando Alonso reportedly wants a €40 million Aston Martin deal through 2028, with a decision expected after the Dutch GP
stories.what_happened: According to multiple F1 market reports on Monday, Alonso is now pushing for a concrete number: **€40 million per season**, a roughly 33% raise on his current pay, in exchange for extending his Aston Martin career through the end of **2028** — by which point he'd be 47. Aston Martin has reportedly already sent him a **Letter of Intent**, a step short of a signed contract but a signal the team wants to close the deal. If finalised at that figure, Alonso would rank as the **third-best-paid driver on the 2027 grid**, behind only Max Verstappen (reported at €70 million) and Lewis Hamilton (€60 million), and level with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc. Reports say Alonso's camp wants **guarantees on future engine upgrades** as part of any deal, not just the salary figure, reflecting his frustration with Aston Martin's underwhelming start to the 2026 rules era. The team and driver are expected to formally announce a decision once F1 returns from its summer break at the Dutch Grand Prix.
key_points: Alonso is said to be seeking **€40 million a season** to stay at Aston Martin — up from his current **€30 million**.
That would make him F1's **third-highest-paid driver**, level with Charles Leclerc and behind only Verstappen and Hamilton.
Aston Martin has reportedly responded with a **Letter of Intent**, signalling serious interest in locking him down.
The proposed deal would keep the **43-year-old racing to age 47**, through the 2027 and 2028 seasons.
An announcement is expected **after the Dutch Grand Prix** (August 21–23), once F1's summer break ends.

depth.background: Fernando Alonso is out of contract with Aston Martin at the end of 2026, and his future has been one of the F1 driver market's biggest open questions all season — team boss **Adrian Newey** said last week he was confident of keeping him, while Alonso himself said he'd decide his future somewhere between the Zandvoort and Monza race weekends. Aston Martin has been investing heavily to turn itself into a front-running team, including a new **Honda works engine partnership** starting in 2026, and Alonso is central to that project both as a driver and as a mentor figure for the team's technical rebuild under Newey.

stories.title: McLaren won't stop developing its 2026 car despite trailing Mercedes in the design race, with a big upgrade for the Azerbaijan GP
stories.what_happened: McLaren confirmed it will **keep developing its 2026 car (the MCL40)** after the summer break rather than pivoting fully to 2027, technical director for applied engineering **Neil Houldey** said. Houldey said the team plans **smaller upgrades** across the first few races back from the break, before bringing a **"significant" package to the Azerbaijan Grand Prix** in Baku in late September. He added there's "a good chance" of further upgrades even after Baku that can extract more performance "without impacting 2027." The team explained its slow start to 2026 stemmed from fending off a late Red Bull title challenge in 2025 and from a mid-development "course correction" on the 2026 car's concept. Next year's rules bring a shorter front floor edge (300mm shorter), among other changes, that will affect how much of this year's learning carries forward.
key_points: McLaren says it's **"certainly not stopping development"** on its 2026 car, even with the title fight still open.
Technical director Neil Houldey confirmed a potentially **"significant" upgrade package** targeted for the **Azerbaijan Grand Prix** in Baku.
McLaren's 2026 car development reportedly ran **about three months behind** Mercedes' this season.
The team says gains made on the 2026 car will **carry over into next year's rules**, so it isn't purely a 2026-only bet.
Piastri leads Norris by **9 points** coming out of the summer break, with Norris on a hot streak — 3 wins in the last 4 races.

depth.background: Every August, F1 teams face a strategic choice at the summer break: keep spending scarce development budget and staff hours on **this year's car**, or shift focus to **next year's**, since 2027 brings a fresh set of technical rules. Teams like **Cadillac** have already said they're abandoning their winless 2026 car entirely to focus on 2027. McLaren enters the break in a tighter spot — its own driver **Oscar Piastri leads the championship by just 9 points** over teammate **Lando Norris**, who has won three of the last four races. McLaren's title defence is real, but the team also privately admits its 2026 car design started about three months behind Mercedes, forcing it to play catch-up all season.

stories.title: Iran hardens its price for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, days after a missile hit a UAE oil tanker there
stories.what_happened: Early on **Saturday**, an Iranian missile struck an ADNOC tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz; the UAE says there were no casualties this time, though the ministry noted that more than a dozen ADNOC vessels have now been hit by missiles or drones since the war began, with one sailor killed and 20 injured across the attacks. The UAE's foreign ministry branded the strike an act of piracy by Iran's **Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)** and called on Tehran to halt the attacks and reopen the strait completely. Separately, Iran's foreign minister said Sunday that Tehran is close to a narrower, temporary arrangement with **Oman** allowing a limited shipping route through the strait — but stressed Iran still wants to largely control it. By Monday, Iranian officials had gone further, publicly setting out preconditions for a full reopening: the US must lift its blockade of Iranian ports, withdraw its forces from the region, drop sanctions on Iran, and pay damages for the war, before Hormuz 'fully reopens.' President Trump, for his part, has signaled he is for now leaning on economic pressure rather than a fresh military offensive.
key_points: Iran now demands the US **lift its blockade of Iranian ports**, withdraw troops, drop sanctions and **pay war damages** before Hormuz fully reopens.
A UAE-flagged **ADNOC oil tanker** was hit by an Iranian missile in the strait in the early hours of **Saturday**; no one was hurt this time.
Since the US-Israel war on Iran began in **February**, over a dozen ADNOC ships have been attacked, leaving **1 crew member dead and 20 wounded**.
The UAE called the strike an **'act of piracy'** by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps and demanded the strait reopen **'fully and unconditionally.'**
Iran's foreign minister separately said Sunday it is close to a **narrower deal with Oman** for a limited shipping route — short of a full reopening.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil and a big share of its liquefied natural gas passes through — making it one of the most important chokepoints in the global economy. Since the **US and Israel launched a war on Iran in February 2026**, Iran has periodically closed or restricted the strait and its forces have repeatedly struck commercial ships passing through it, including tankers belonging to **ADNOC**, Abu Dhabi's state oil company. Earlier this month Iran and Oman appeared to be closing in on an arrangement that would let some shipping resume under agreed coordinates, raising hopes the crisis could ease.

thread.previously: We reported Iran and Oman had agreed on shipping-lane coordinates through the Strait of Hormuz, with a limited-access deal appearing close to completion.
thread.changed: Iran has now attached hard new preconditions — a lifted blockade on its ports, a full US troop withdrawal, dropped sanctions, and war damages — before it will fully reopen the strait, even as a missile hit a UAE oil tanker there over the weekend.

stories.title: Isack Hadjar calls his jump from Racing Bulls to Red Bull a 'culture shock' — from family Italian team to British operation
stories.what_happened: Speaking on the Talking Bull podcast during F1's summer shutdown, Isack Hadjar described the jump from Racing Bulls to the senior Red Bull team as a genuine **'culture shock.'** "That's definitely a culture shock, let's say," he said. "You go from more of a family team, an Italian team, to British. It's definitely different." Despite the adjustment in team culture and environment, Hadjar said the actual technical transition felt natural, since he has been part of Red Bull's junior driver pipeline since 2021 and had already worked with his current race engineer, known as 'Woody,' during junior testing and FP1 (Free Practice 1) sessions three years before his 2026 promotion.
key_points: **Isack Hadjar**, 21, says stepping up from Racing Bulls to partner Max Verstappen at Red Bull this year has been a **'culture shock.'**
He described Racing Bulls as **'more of a family team, an Italian team'** versus Red Bull's British operation — 'it's definitely different.'
Despite the adjustment, Hadjar says the move has felt **natural** because he's been in Red Bull's junior pipeline since **2021**.
He'd already worked with his current race engineer **'Woody'** during junior testing and FP1 outings three years before the promotion.
The comments came on the **Talking Bull podcast**, during F1's mandatory summer shutdown.

depth.background: F1 teams run a two-tier structure for many manufacturers: Red Bull's junior squad, Racing Bulls (formerly AlphaTauri/Toro Rosso), is based in Italy's Faenza and has historically had a more informal, close-knit culture, while the senior Red Bull Racing team is headquartered in Milton Keynes, England, and runs a larger, more corporate operation built around competing for championships. Hadjar spent his rookie 2025 season with Racing Bulls before being promoted to partner four-time champion Max Verstappen at the senior team for 2026 — a high-pressure seat given Verstappen's stature and Red Bull's championship expectations. F1 is currently in its mandatory 14-day summer shutdown (August 3–17), during which teams must pause car development, leaving driver interviews and reflective content as the main news flow.

stories.title: Western Europe just logged its hottest June–July ever, as wildfires burn over a million acres
stories.what_happened: The EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service confirmed Monday that western Europe's June and July 2026 was, on average, the hottest two-month opening to summer ever recorded, at 21.62°C — about 2.79°C above the historical average and above the previous record set in 2022. Separately, Copernicus said July 2026 was the hottest month ever logged for the world's oceans outside the polar regions, with record highs along the Atlantic and western Mediterranean. The extreme heat has fed record-breaking wildfires across Spain, France, and Italy, which together have burned more than 1.23 million acres and displaced hundreds of thousands of people, according to an EU report from August 6. Scientists point to abnormally dry soil — moisture levels in western Europe were significantly lower this July than in the previous record year of 2022 — as a key reason the heat has translated so directly into fire.
key_points: Western Europe's **June–July 2026** was its **hottest ever recorded** two-month stretch, per the EU's Copernicus climate monitor.
Average temperature hit **21.62°C**, about **2.79°C above** the long-term average — beating the previous record set in **2022**.
**July was the hottest month ever logged** for the world's non-polar oceans, with record highs in the Atlantic and western Mediterranean.
Wildfires have burned over **1.23 million acres**, mostly in **Spain, France, and Italy**, displacing hundreds of thousands of people.

depth.background: Copernicus is the European Union's official climate-monitoring service, tracking global temperature and ocean heat using satellites and ground sensors. Europe has been warming roughly twice as fast as the global average for decades, a trend scientists link to its geography and shrinking snow and ice cover. Spain and France are already living through their worst wildfire seasons on record this year, as repeated heatwaves dry out soil and vegetation, priming them to burn faster and hotter each time.

stories.title: Parliament's final week opens with a new FCRA bill row as Opposition protests force an adjournment
stories.what_happened: Parliament entered its final week of the Monsoon Session on Monday with no resolution to the multi-day stand-off over Amit Shah's statement on the student-protest crackdown. The Lok Sabha introduced four bills — the **Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026**, the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill 2026**, the **Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill 2026**, and the **National Co-operative Development Corporation (Amendment) Bill 2026** — but before substantive debate could proceed, vociferous Opposition protests forced the Speaker to adjourn the House until 2 PM. Separately, Congress and other Opposition parties signaled they will strongly resist a proposed amendment to the **FCRA**, the law governing foreign funding of Indian organizations, if the government tables it this week. With only four sitting days left in the session, the combination of the ongoing Shah stand-off and the new FCRA fight leaves little room for the government's remaining legislative agenda.
key_points: Lok Sabha proceedings were **adjourned till 2 PM** on Monday amid Opposition protests over Amit Shah's silence on the student-protest crackdown.
The government introduced **four new bills**, including the **Tribunals Reforms Bill** and an amendment to India's **Mines and Minerals Act**.
The Opposition says it will strongly protest if the government's **FCRA (foreign funding) bill** amendment is formally tabled this week.
Only **four sitting days remain** in the Monsoon Session, sharply limiting how much legislative business can still get done.
This is the **same underlying stand-off** as last week — Shah's presence on the crackdown issue — with a new bill fight layered on top.

depth.background: India's Parliament holds three sessions a year; the Monsoon Session typically runs through July and August and is where the government pushes through a backlog of bills before the year's final Winter Session. This year's session has been dominated by Opposition anger over a police crackdown on student protesters — parties including Congress have been demanding Home Minister Amit Shah personally address the House on it, and the government's refusal (or delay) has repeatedly stalled proceedings. FCRA — the **Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act** — governs how NGOs and other Indian organizations can receive funding from abroad; past amendments to it have been controversial because critics say tightening it can be used to squeeze civil-society and activist groups that rely on foreign donors.

thread.previously: We reported Parliament entering its last week of the Monsoon Session deadlocked, with the Opposition pressing Home Minister Amit Shah for an explanation of a police crackdown on student protesters.
thread.changed: Monday added a second flashpoint: the government introduced four bills, including a new **FCRA (foreign funding law) amendment** the Opposition says it will fight, and repeated protests forced the Lok Sabha to adjourn until 2 PM — showing the deadlock hasn't eased with just four sitting days left.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll crosses 100 as monsoon devastation deepens
stories.what_happened: Assam's flood death toll has climbed past **100**, according to the State Disaster Management Authority, up from 99 reported the previous day. The toll includes 60 males, 23 females, and 18 children. **Cachar district** has the highest count with 22 deaths, with further fatalities spread across Sivasagar, Darrang, Nagaon, Dibrugarh, Hailakandi, Hojai, Kamrup, and Lakhimpur districts. More than **1.4 to 1.6 lakh people** remain affected across over a dozen districts, with homes, farmland, and infrastructure inundated. Relief operations continue through more than 2,000 distribution centres, with tens of thousands of people still sheltered in relief camps.
key_points: Assam's flood death toll has **crossed 100**, up from 99 a day earlier.
Deaths break down as **60 males, 23 females, and 18 children**, per the state disaster authority.
**Cachar district** has recorded the most deaths (22), followed by Sivasagar and other northeastern districts.
Over **1.4-1.6 lakh people** remain affected across more than a dozen districts.
CM **Himanta Biswa Sarma** has been touring breached embankments, including in Darrang district.

depth.background: Assam floods almost every monsoon season because the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swell with heavy rain and glacial melt from the Himalayas, regularly breaching embankments across the state's low-lying floodplains. This year's flooding has been especially severe, with the death toll climbing steadily through late July and August as successive waves of heavy rain hit an already-saturated state. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has been visiting the worst-hit districts, including Darrang, to inspect embankment breaches and relief efforts.

stories.title: Israeli fire wounds 7 Palestinians in Gaza on the ceasefire's fifth day, as the truce's death toll passes 1,250
stories.what_happened: On Sunday, August 10, Israeli forces opened fire in southern and central **Khan Younis**, wounding 7 Palestinians — including a woman and a child — six of whom were taken to Nasser Hospital. Israeli tanks separately fired on tents sheltering displaced people in **Al-Mawasi**, a coastal strip Israel has designated a 'safe zone' but which has been hit repeatedly during the ceasefire period. Military vehicles and drones also fired on homes and tents in the eastern Al-Tuffah neighborhood the same day. Gaza's Health Ministry says these incidents are part of a much larger pattern: since the ceasefire took effect, it counts **over 1,257 Palestinians killed and over 4,131 wounded** by what it classifies as Israeli violations. This comes as talks are due to resume on August 15 over the next phase — full Hamas disarmament — which Israel has made a precondition for any troop withdrawal.
key_points: **7 Palestinians wounded**, including a woman and child, after Israeli forces opened fire in **Khan Younis** on Sunday.
Israeli **tanks fired on tents** sheltering displaced families in Al-Mawasi, between Khan Younis and Rafah.
Gaza's Health Ministry says ceasefire violations have killed **over 1,257 Palestinians** and wounded **over 4,131** since the truce began in October.
Hamas says it won't fully disarm until Israel halts attacks and withdraws troops — Israel says no withdrawal until disarmament is verified.
It's a **stand-off**: each side is waiting on the other to move first, and civilians are absorbing the violence in between.

depth.background: The Gaza ceasefire took effect in **October 2025** after a US-brokered deal, and on paper it has held for months — no return to full-scale war. But 'ceasefire' has never meant 'zero violence' here: both sides have accused each other of near-daily breaches, from Israeli strikes on people near the security line it still controls, to sporadic Hamas activity. In July, President Trump announced what he called a 'historic agreement' for Hamas and other armed groups to disarm, but Hamas has refused to move first, saying Israel must halt attacks and withdraw troops — obligations Israel says it won't meet until disarmament is independently verified. That disagreement is the entire ceasefire in miniature: a truce that holds in name while neither side fully complies with what got it signed.

thread.previously: We reported the ceasefire was holding into its fifth day, with pressure building on Hamas to begin disarming and Israel due to resume ceasefire talks on August 15.
thread.changed: Even as the truce technically 'holds,' Israeli fire on Sunday wounded 7 Palestinians in Khan Younis and Al-Mawasi — a reminder that 'holding' doesn't mean quiet. Gaza's Health Ministry now says ceasefire-period violations have killed over 1,250 Palestinians and wounded over 4,100 since it began.

stories.title: RBI steps in to defend the rupee as rising oil prices threaten to push it past 95.4/dollar
stories.what_happened: The Indian rupee looked set to open weaker on Monday, sliding toward **95.35–95.40 per dollar**, as a fresh rise in oil prices revived worries about India's oil import bill and inflation outlook. **Brent crude rose 1.3% to $83.6 a barrel**, extending gains for a third straight session. Traders said the **Reserve Bank of India stepped in right around the market open**, selling dollars to slow the rupee's slide, which left the currency little changed at around **95.26–95.27 per dollar** instead. This continues a pattern of RBI intervention reported through the prior week as oil prices climbed on Middle East tensions, including the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
key_points: The rupee was on track to open near **95.35–95.40 per dollar** on Monday before RBI intervention pulled it back.
**Brent crude climbed to $83.6 a barrel**, up 1.3%, extending a multi-day rise on Middle East tensions.
Costlier oil is a direct threat to India, which imports **over 85% of its crude oil needs**.
The RBI is estimated to have sold dollars right at market open to **cushion the rupee's fall** — a now-recurring pattern this month.
The rupee has weakened **8.6% over the past year**, even after strengthening slightly over the past month.

depth.background: India imports the vast majority of the oil it uses, so **when global crude prices rise, more dollars have to flow out of India to pay for it** — which weakens the rupee. The rupee has been under pressure through 2026 from a mix of costly oil, trade-tariff uncertainty with the US, and foreign investors periodically pulling money out of Indian markets. The RBI doesn't let the rupee move freely; it periodically buys or sells dollars in the market to smooth out sharp swings, a practice traders infer from sudden reversals in the exchange rate rather than official announcements. This is the same oil-price move tied to this week's Strait of Hormuz and Iran tanker tensions.

stories.title: Sensex opens flat, Nifty holds above 24,500 as strong global cues offset a quiet start to the week
stories.what_happened: Indian benchmark indices opened Monday on a **mildly positive note**, extending the momentum from strong global cues. The Sensex opened up just 2.42 points at 78,501.59, essentially flat, while the Nifty 50 added 10.6 points to open at 24,581.25, staying comfortably above the 24,500 level. The early Gift Nifty indicator — a proxy that trades ahead of the domestic market open — had signaled a stronger open, up 45 points at 24,686.50, suggesting some of the initial enthusiasm faded once cash-market trading began. Asian markets broadly traded higher overnight, following gains on Wall Street on Friday after a weaker-than-expected US jobs report reduced the odds of near-term Fed rate hikes. On the Sensex, **Titan, ICICI Bank, HCL Tech, Infosys and SBI** led the gainers, with Titan up about 1.01% in early trade. Institutional flow data showed Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) bought a net Rs 480.24 crore of Indian equities on August 7, while Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs) bought Rs 235.56 crore.
key_points: The **BSE Sensex** opened nearly flat, up just **2.42 points** at 78,501.59.
The **Nifty 50** gained **10.6 points** to open at **24,581.25**, holding above the psychologically important 24,500 level.
**Titan, ICICI Bank, HCL Tech, Infosys and SBI** led early gainers on the Sensex.
**Asian markets traded higher** overnight, tracking Wall Street's Friday gains after a weak US jobs report cooled fears of near-term Fed tightening.
**Foreign investors bought Rs 480 crore** of Indian equities on August 7, while domestic institutions added Rs 236 crore.

depth.background: Indian markets have been closely tracking US Federal Reserve signals in recent weeks: a weaker-than-expected US jobs report last week reduced fears the Fed would raise rates in September, which lifted risk appetite globally, including in Asia. India's own market mood has also been buoyed by foreign investors returning as buyers after a stretch where they were net sellers, alongside domestic institutional investors who have been steady buyers for months. Sensex and Nifty are widely watched as India's two main stock benchmarks — the Sensex tracks 30 large companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange, the Nifty 50 tracks 50 large companies on the National Stock Exchange.

stories.title: Oscar Piastri warned he risks becoming McLaren's 'number two' as Lando Norris pulls ahead
stories.what_happened: Formula 1 commentator David Croft said Piastri needs to find a way to match Norris's pace or risk McLaren effectively treating him as the team's number two driver, even without an official declaration. The comments come as Norris has pulled ahead of his teammate across recent races heading into F1's mid-season **summer break**, raising questions about whether McLaren will keep its stated equal-treatment policy if the performance gap widens further. McLaren has not signaled any change to its approach, and both drivers remain in the fight for the drivers' championship, but the widening internal gap is becoming a bigger storyline than the external title race for some observers.
key_points: F1 pundit David Croft warned Piastri risks being seen as McLaren's **'number two' driver**.
Norris has been **outpacing Piastri** through the recent run of races heading into the summer break.
The concern: will McLaren informally **prioritize Norris** in the title fight if the gap keeps growing?
McLaren has repeatedly insisted it treats both drivers **equally**, unlike some rival teams.
The tension adds a subplot to F1's four-week **summer break**, when driver-market talks typically heat up.

depth.background: McLaren went into the 2026 season with Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri as a nominally equal driver pairing, both racing for the constructors' and drivers' titles without a designated team leader — a policy the team has publicly stood by even as rivals like Red Bull have historically favored one driver. Through the season, Norris has increasingly out-qualified and out-raced his teammate, raising the perennial F1 question of whether a team with two title-capable drivers can keep treating them as truly equal once one clearly has the upper hand.

stories.title: The contiguous US just recorded its hottest month ever, breaking Dust Bowl-era and 2012 heat records
stories.what_happened: NOAA announced that **July 2026** was the hottest month ever recorded across the contiguous United States, narrowly beating the prior records set in **July 1936** and **July 2012** by **0.1 to 0.2°F**. The national average temperature for the month came in at **76.9°F**, **3.3°F** above the 20th-century average, with warmer-than-normal conditions affecting the entire contiguous US. Nighttime low temperatures broke their own record by **0.7°F**, a sign this heat wasn't just scorching afternoons but relentless overnight warmth too. The month was marked by a cluster of extreme weather — heat waves, drought, severe storms, flash flooding and wildfires — hitting nearly every corner of the country during July.
key_points: **July 2026** was the hottest month for the contiguous US since record-keeping began in **1895** — **132 years** of data.
The national average temperature hit **76.9°F**, **3.3°F** above the 20th-century average.
It edged out the previous records set in **July 1936** (Dust Bowl era) and **July 2012**.
Nighttime low temperatures — crucial for people and crops to recover from daytime heat — broke their own record by **0.7°F**.
The month brought a wave of heat waves, drought, severe storms, flooding and wildfires to nearly every region of the country.

depth.background: NOAA's **National Centers for Environmental Information** has tracked US temperatures since **1895**, giving scientists a long baseline for judging how unusual any given month really is. Until now, the record for hottest month was shared by **July 1936**, during the Dust Bowl drought, and **July 2012**, a year of severe Midwest drought and crop failure. Climate scientists have long said human-caused warming is loading the dice toward more frequent, more extreme heat months on top of ordinary year-to-year variation, and warm nights are considered especially dangerous because bodies, animals and crops don't get the overnight cool-down that normally limits heat stress.

stories.title: Trump signs executive order to split the MMR vaccine into three shots and cut required childhood vaccinations
stories.what_happened: On **August 10**, President Trump signed an executive order titled "Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations," directing federal health agencies to cut the number of universally recommended childhood vaccine doses from **17 to 11** and to space shots out across separate doctor visits rather than bundling them. Its centerpiece is a push to break the combined **MMR vaccine** into three individual shots, even though no such separated vaccine is currently approved or manufactured in the US — doing so would require drugmakers to run fresh clinical trials and win FDA approval, a process that typically takes years. Medical groups including the **American College of Physicians** immediately pushed back, warning the order bypasses normal scientific review, while the **CDC** itself noted there is no published evidence that splitting the shot helps anyone. Public-health experts warn that adding extra required clinic visits could actually lower vaccination completion rates, particularly for lower-income families for whom each visit is a real logistical and financial cost.
key_points: Trump signed a **"Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations"** executive order on **August 10**, aiming to cut universally recommended childhood shots from **17 to 11**.
The order calls for splitting the combined **MMR (measles-mumps-rubella)** vaccine into **three separate shots** given at separate visits.
The **CDC itself says** there is **"no published scientific evidence"** that separating the MMR shot has any benefit.
Standalone measles, mumps and rubella vaccines don't currently exist in the US — makers would need **new clinical trials** and FDA approval first.
The **American College of Physicians** accused the administration of bypassing the transparent scientific review that has guided vaccine policy for decades.

depth.background: Since Trump's second term began, his administration has repeatedly pushed to slim down and space out the US childhood immunization schedule, arguing — without mainstream scientific backing — that today's schedule is too aggressive. The combined **MMR vaccine** has been standard since the 1970s specifically because giving three protections in one shot means fewer clinic visits and higher completion rates, which is why public-health bodies see splitting it apart as a step backward, not forward. Health agencies have already seen repeated leadership turnover and internal disputes over vaccine guidance this year, and this order revives that fight just as children head back to school.

stories.title: F1 rewrites its 2027-28 engine rules after Verstappen-led driver backlash over 'artificial' racing
stories.what_happened: The FIA's **World Motor Sport Council** formally ratified new F1 power-unit rules for 2027 and 2028, shifting the combustion-to-electric power split from today's roughly **53/47** to **58/42** next year and **60/40** the year after. Under the change, the maximum output of the electric **MGU-K** falls from **350kW to 300kW**, while the combustion engine's peak power rises to **420kW in 2027** and **450kW in 2028**, with the fuel-flow rate increasing by **5%** and **13%** respectively to support that extra combustion power. The changes are a direct response to driver complaints, led loudest by four-time champion **Max Verstappen**, who said earlier this year he could walk away from F1 if the battery-management-heavy formula wasn't fixed. On **August 10**, F1 CEO **Stefano Domenicali** confirmed he'd held "constructive" talks with Verstappen about the sport's direction as the rule change was finalized, tying the regulatory shift directly to retaining the sport's biggest star.
key_points: The FIA ratified a shift from today's roughly **53/47** combustion-to-electric power split to **58/42 in 2027** and **60/40 in 2028**.
Maximum electric power from the **MGU-K** drops from **350kW to 300kW**, while combustion engine power rises to **420kW (2027)** and **450kW (2028)**.
The change directly answers driver complaints — led by **Max Verstappen** — that managing battery energy in qualifying made racing feel artificial and unsafe.
Verstappen had **threatened to leave F1** if the rules weren't changed for next year.
F1 boss **Stefano Domenicali** confirmed talks with Verstappen on **August 10** as the sport finalized the changes.

depth.background: F1's current hybrid engines, introduced for the 2026 season, gave the electric motor (the **MGU-K**) an unusually large share of total power — a roughly **50-50 split** with the combustion engine — to push the sport toward greater electrification. In practice, drivers found that managing the battery's limited energy supply during a single qualifying lap forced unnatural driving styles, like coasting off-throttle mid-corner just to save energy, which several drivers, Verstappen most vocally, called dangerous and "artificial." The backlash built through the first half of the 2026 season as drivers and teams lobbied the FIA to rebalance the engine formula before it locked in for years.

stories.title: An unreleased Claude research model pushes a 160-year-old math problem's bound from 41.6% to 67.2%
stories.what_happened: Anthropic said on **August 10** that an unreleased research version of its Claude AI model improved a decades-old mathematical bound connected to the Riemann hypothesis, raising the proportion of zeta-function zeros proven to lie on the 'critical line' from **41.6% to 67.2%** — the largest single jump on this specific figure in the problem's history. Claude reached the result over **two extended coding sessions**, coordinating roughly **60 subagents** and generating about **31 million tokens** of output as it studied prior research, tested ideas, wrote code and checked its own results. Anthropic's mathematicians reviewed the work, outside experts examined the paper, and Claude additionally produced a machine-checkable version of the proof using the formal-verification language **Lean 4**. The company published the manuscript, the Lean repository and its process logs publicly, though the underlying model itself remains unreleased, with no weights disclosed. Crucially, Claude did not prove the Riemann hypothesis itself — a lower bound of 67.2% is still very far from the 100% a full proof would need, and no known technique, human or machine, currently exists to close that gap.
key_points: Anthropic disclosed that an **unreleased, research-only version of Claude** made the largest single jump ever recorded on a bound tied to the **Riemann hypothesis**.
The AI raised the proven lower bound on zeta-function zeros lying on the 'critical line' from **41.6% to 67.2%**.
The work used **two extended coding sessions**, roughly **60 subagents**, and **31 million output tokens**.
Human mathematicians reviewed the result, and Claude also produced a machine-checkable proof using the formal-verification tool **Lean**.
The Riemann hypothesis itself remains **unsolved** — 67.2% is still far short of the 100% a full proof would require.

depth.background: The **Riemann hypothesis** is one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics, first proposed in 1859, with a **$1 million Millennium Prize** attached to a full proof. It makes a precise claim about where the zeros of a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function are located — a claim that, if true, would explain deep patterns in how prime numbers are distributed. Mathematicians have long tried to prove that a growing *fraction* of these zeros satisfy the hypothesis, even without proving it for all of them; that fraction is the 'bound' this AI system just moved. Anthropic ran this as an internal research exercise using a version of its Claude model that has not been released to the public.

stories.title: Sharad Pawar's party meets Modi as India's next Lok Sabha seat count sparks a north-south political fight
stories.what_happened: All eight Lok Sabha MPs of the Sharad Pawar-led NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar), headed by working president **Supriya Sule**, met Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** at his residence on **Monday**. The meeting, which lasted roughly 15-30 minutes by different accounts, was officially about **Maharashtra-specific issues** — drought, water scarcity, onion prices, and pollution in the Chandrabhaga river — and constituency concerns. But it took place amid active speculation that the party might be softening its opposition to the **Delimitation Bill** or edging closer to the ruling NDA coalition, given Parliament's disrupted monsoon session has left many MPs unable to raise issues on the floor. Sule pushed back on the political read, saying no political topics were discussed and that the meeting was simply a practical way to escalate constituency issues directly to the PM. Congress and other opposition parties, wary of any crack in the anti-delimitation front, have been pushing allied parties to hold a firm, unified line.
key_points: All **8 Lok Sabha MPs** of the Sharad Pawar-led NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar), led by **Supriya Sule**, met PM Modi at his residence.
The meeting fuelled speculation the party could **soften its stance** on India's upcoming **Delimitation Bill**.
**Delimitation** would redraw parliamentary seats based on population — potentially shifting power toward the **north** and away from southern/western states.
Sule said the meeting was a **courtesy call** about local Maharashtra issues, not politics, since Parliament sittings have been disrupted.
Opposition parties, including **Congress**, want NCP(SP) to hold a firm, unified anti-delimitation line.

depth.background: India's Constitution froze the number of Lok Sabha seats by state in the 1970s specifically so that states which controlled population growth (mostly in the south and west) wouldn't be punished with fewer seats relative to faster-growing northern states. That freeze was meant to be temporary and is due to end after the next census-based delimitation exercise, which is why the topic is now explosive: a straightforward population-based reallocation could shift dozens of seats toward states like Uttar Pradesh and Bihar and away from Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Maharashtra. **Supriya Sule** leads the parliamentary wing of the NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar), the faction led by veteran leader **Sharad Pawar** after the party split from Ajit Pawar's NCP faction, which is part of the ruling NDA coalition. Delimitation has already become a flashpoint in this year's Parliament session.

stories.title: Jharkhand protest leader hospitalized in critical condition after 9-day hunger strike over exam scam
stories.what_happened: Devendra Nath Mahto, the 33-year-old leader of Jharkhand's student job-exam protests, was hospitalized on **Monday** after his blood sugar dropped sharply while he joined a march toward the state legislative assembly — arriving on a stretcher after **nine days** without food. Doctors at Ranchi Sadar Hospital described his condition as **critical**. His hospitalization came the same day riot police used water cannons and batons on protesters marching on the assembly building, and at least **six other protesters** remain on indefinite hunger strike despite the escalating health toll. The state government had already moved over the weekend to cancel the 14th JPSC preliminary exam and two backlog recruitment tests, and three JPSC board members resigned after being questioned by state investigators. But student groups say the protest will continue until the government also scraps the separate Combined Graduate Level exam and hands the paper-leak investigation to the CBI, which they don't yet trust the state to run impartially.
key_points: Student leader **Devendra Nath Mahto**, 33, was hospitalized after his **blood sugar dropped drastically** during Monday's march.
He had been on an **indefinite hunger strike for nine days**, protesting alleged **recruitment exam irregularities** in Jharkhand.
Doctors at **Ranchi Sadar Hospital** described his condition as **critical**.
At least **six other protesters** remain on hunger strike even after his hospitalization.
The state government has already agreed to **cancel three tainted exams**, but protesters want the **CBI** to take over the probe.

depth.background: The protest began after allegations surfaced that recruitment exams run by the **Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC)** and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission were compromised by paper leaks and rigging, threatening the futures of thousands of young job-seekers in one of India's poorer states. Student leader **Devendra Nath Mahto** emerged as the face of the movement, going on hunger strike to press the government to scrap the tainted exams and hand the investigation to India's federal police agency, the **Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)**. The state government has already cancelled the 14th JPSC preliminary exam and two backlog recruitment tests, and three JPSC board members resigned after being questioned by investigators, but protesters say that isn't enough.

stories.title: Indian physicist Deepak Dhar wins the 2026 Dirac Medal for statistical mechanics work
stories.what_happened: The ICTP announced that Deepak Dhar is one of **four recipients of the 2026 Dirac Medal**, alongside Bernard Derrida, Marc Mézard and Haim Sompolinsky. The citation credits the four for **transforming concepts from equilibrium statistical mechanics** — the physics of systems in balance — **into tools used far beyond physics**, including optimisation problems, theoretical neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Dhar is specifically recognised for his work on **self-organised criticality** and the **abelian sandpile model**, mathematical frameworks that explain why some systems (like sandpiles, or by extension earthquakes and market crashes) naturally organise themselves to the edge of instability, where small triggers can cause disproportionately large events. With this award, Dhar becomes the **first scientist to hold both the Dirac Medal and the 2022 Boltzmann Medal**, another top honour in statistical physics.
key_points: **Deepak Dhar**, formerly of IISER Pune and TIFR, wins the **2026 Dirac Medal**, one of physics' highest honours.
He shares it with **Bernard Derrida, Marc Mézard and Haim Sompolinsky** for work spanning statistical mechanics.
Dhar is honoured for pioneering **self-organised criticality** and the **abelian sandpile model**.
He becomes the **first person to hold both the Dirac Medal and the Boltzmann Medal** (won in 2022).
The medal is awarded by the **ICTP** (Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics) in Trieste, Italy.

depth.background: The **Dirac Medal**, instituted in 1985 by the ICTP and named after Nobel laureate Paul Dirac, is considered one of the most prestigious prizes in theoretical physics — past winners include **Stephen Hawking**. It recognises physicists whose work has had a broad, lasting influence across the field, rather than a single discovery. Dhar built his career largely in India, at the **Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR)**, **IISER Pune**, and the **International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS) Bengaluru**, working on the mathematics of complex, disordered systems — the kind of physics that describes everything from avalanches to earthquakes to financial crashes.

stories.title: ICC confirms 12 venues across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia for the 2027 Cricket World Cup
stories.what_happened: The **International Cricket Council (ICC)** formally confirmed the **12 venues** for the 2027 Men's Cricket World Cup, unveiling the host cities and tournament brand in a launch ceremony. **South Africa** will host the bulk of the tournament across **8 grounds** — Wanderers Stadium (Johannesburg), SuperSport Park (Centurion), Newlands (Cape Town), Kingsmead (Durban), St George's Park (Gqeberha), Mangaung Oval (Bloemfontein), Boland Park (Paarl) and Buffalo Park (East London). **Zimbabwe** contributes **3 venues** — Harare Sports Club, Queens Sports Club in Bulawayo, and the newly constructed **Mosi-oa-Tunya International Cricket Stadium** in Victoria Falls, built specifically for this tournament. **Namibia** hosts matches at its **National Cricket Ground in Windhoek**. In total, **14 teams** will contest **57 matches**, and the event marks the tournament's first trip to Africa since South Africa hosted alone in 2003.
key_points: The **2027 Men's Cricket World Cup** will be co-hosted by **South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia**.
**14 teams** will play **57 matches** across the tournament.
**South Africa hosts 8 venues**, including Wanderers (Johannesburg), Newlands (Cape Town) and Centurion.
**Zimbabwe gets 3 venues**, including the newly built **Mosi-oa-Tunya Stadium** in Victoria Falls.
It's the tournament's **first return to Africa since 2003**, when South Africa last hosted.

depth.background: The Cricket World Cup rotates among cricket's major nations, and Africa has hosted only once before — **South Africa in 2003**. Zimbabwe and Namibia have never hosted a men's World Cup match at this scale; folding them into a joint hosting arrangement with South Africa is partly about **spreading the sport's growth and infrastructure investment** across the region, similar to how football's World Cup has occasionally used multi-country hosting.

stories.title: Red Bull admits F1's budget cap will slow the RB22's recovery for the rest of 2026
stories.what_happened: Red Bull team principal **Laurent Mekies** acknowledged this week that the team's **budget cap** will limit how much it can improve the **RB22** for the rest of 2026, effectively locking in a difficult season. He said the team is **'paying the price'** for pushing development of last year's RB21 deep into late 2025, which left less of this year's capped budget available to fix the RB22's problems once they emerged. Multiple reports say Red Bull has **internally accepted the RB22 is a 'flop'**, even with half the season still to go, pointing specifically to aerodynamic issues around the car's rear wing that have hurt both Verstappen and teammate Isack Hadjar. The team introduced two upgrade packages already this year (Miami and Austria) and shed excess weight, but Mekies said further big changes are now constrained by the cap, forcing a choice between **fixing 2026 or protecting the 2027 budget**. Red Bull currently sits **fourth in the constructors' championship**, more than 200 points behind leader Mercedes, with all four of its podium finishes coming from Verstappen alone.
key_points: Red Bull team principal **Laurent Mekies** admits the team is **'paying the price'** for a 2025 development gamble.
The team kept developing its **old RB21 car deep into late 2025**, leaving less budget for the new RB22.
F1's **budget cap is $215 million** this year, and aerodynamic-testing limits restrict how much catch-up is possible.
The **RB22 is regarded internally as a 'flop'**, even with half the season still to run.
Red Bull sits **fourth in the constructors' standings**, all four podiums so far coming from Max Verstappen alone.

depth.background: Since 2021, F1 has run under a **cost cap** ($215 million this season) designed to stop the richest teams from simply outspending rivals into submission — every dollar a team spends on this year's car is a dollar it can't spend on fixing a mistake or preparing for next year's rule changes. Teams also face **aerodynamic testing limits** tied to their championship position: teams lower in the standings actually get **more** wind-tunnel time, a rule meant to help struggling teams catch up. Red Bull chose to keep developing its **2025 car (RB21)** later into last season than most rivals, betting that gains there would carry into 2026 — a bet that has not paid off as hoped.

stories.title: Zuckerberg publishes 6,500-word manifesto pushing 'personal superintelligence' over centralized AI control
stories.what_happened: On August 10, Zuckerberg posted a lengthy personal essay setting out a philosophy for how advanced AI should be built and distributed. He wrote that **invention, not automation, will be the greatest contribution of superintelligence** — AI's job is to hand ordinary people new tools, not just replace their labor. He proposed that frontier AI labs, likely including Meta itself, give the **US government early access to intermediate model checkpoints** (unfinished snapshots of a model, taken before it is publicly released) so officials can assess and prepare for emerging risks to critical infrastructure before a model goes live. He also announced Meta will keep releasing open-weight models, launch a **$1 billion 'Future is for Everyone' fund** to invest in communities near its data centers, and hand model-safety sign-off to Meta's independent board rather than keeping that authority with himself.
key_points: Meta CEO **Mark Zuckerberg** published a **6,500-word essay** titled 'The Future is for Everyone' on August 10.
He proposes frontier AI labs share **unreleased model checkpoints** with the **US government** before public launch.
Meta pledges a new **$1 billion fund** for communities that host its data centers.
Meta's **independent board**, not Zuckerberg personally, will now approve the safety criteria for releasing new AI models.
The essay argues AI's goal should be **individual empowerment through invention**, not automation that replaces jobs.

depth.background: Meta has bet its future on AI, spending tens of billions of dollars on data centers and chips while pushing 'open-weight' models (versions with their underlying settings published so anyone can run or modify them) instead of the closed, subscription-style models sold by rivals like OpenAI and Google. That strategy has drawn criticism as Meta's own flagship models have lagged competitors on some benchmarks, even as the company insists openness is safer than letting a handful of firms control the most powerful AI. Zuckerberg has increasingly positioned himself as AI's leading advocate for **decentralizing power**, arguing concentrated control — by governments or by a few companies — is the bigger long-term risk. The essay lands as governments worldwide are drafting AI safety rules and frontier labs face growing pressure to prove they can self-regulate.

stories.title: Afghanistan beat Ireland to clinch the ODI series and book a direct spot at the 2027 World Cup
stories.what_happened: Afghanistan beat Ireland by **3 wickets** in the 3rd ODI in Belfast on August 10, successfully chasing down Ireland's total with **31 balls to spare**. The win gave Afghanistan an unassailable **2-0 series lead** (after the first match was abandoned to rain) and, with it, direct qualification for the **2027 ODI World Cup** — avoiding a separate qualifying tournament. **Rashid Khan** was a key figure across the series, having taken a **six-wicket haul** in the 2nd ODI alongside a strong batting contribution from Ibrahim Zadran. The series continues with two more dead-rubber matches before it concludes on August 14.
key_points: Afghanistan beat Ireland by **3 wickets** in the 3rd ODI in Belfast, sealing the series **2-0**.
The win secures Afghanistan's **direct qualification for the 2027 ODI World Cup**, sparing them a qualifying tournament.
Leg-spinner **Rashid Khan** was central to the campaign, having taken a **six-wicket haul** in the 2nd ODI.
Afghanistan chased down Ireland's total with **31 balls to spare** in the decisive match.
The result caps a dominant series for Afghanistan, one of the format's fastest-rising teams.

depth.background: Afghanistan have become one of the most competitive white-ball teams in world cricket over the past decade, built around a core of skilled spin bowlers led by **Rashid Khan**, one of the format's best leg-spinners. Direct qualification for the 50-over **ODI World Cup** is determined by teams' rankings and performance in the current cycle — missing it means playing in a separate, high-pressure qualifying tournament against other associate and lower-ranked nations, so a direct spot removes a major source of risk two years out from the 2027 tournament. Ireland, an associate-turned-full-member nation, hosted Afghanistan for a five-match ODI series this month, giving both sides valuable rankings points and match practice.

thread.changed: Afghanistan won that match by 3 wickets, clinching the series 2-0 and securing direct qualification for the 2027 ODI World Cup.

stories.title: Toto Wolff says Kimi Antonelli's rapid rise is 'the best I've seen' from any young F1 driver
stories.what_happened: In comments to RacingNews365, Wolff said Antonelli's growth this season is **"the best I've seen from any young driver in terms of the growing process going so quickly."** Asked what specifically surprised him, Wolff said **"the whole thing is a surprise,"** pointing to Antonelli's ability to take in new information, process it, and execute it on track almost immediately — a skill that normally takes rookies much longer to develop. Antonelli heads into the summer break as the **youngest points leader in F1 history**, having outperformed far more experienced teammates and rivals through the first half of the season. Wolff's comments come alongside Mercedes' plans to bring a **significant car upgrade** after the break to help extend Antonelli's championship lead over Ferrari and other rivals.
key_points: Mercedes boss **Toto Wolff** said 19-year-old **Kimi Antonelli's** growth this season is **"the best I've seen"** from any young driver.
Antonelli currently **leads the F1 drivers' championship** heading into the summer break, the youngest points leader in the sport's history.
Wolff said what surprised him most was Antonelli's **"capability of taking information in, processing it, and executing it."**
Wolff described the trajectory — rookie to title contender in one season — as **a surprise even to the team**.
The comments come as Mercedes eyes a **major car upgrade** after the summer break to help Antonelli defend the points lead.

depth.background: **Kimi Antonelli** is a 19-year-old Italian driver who joined Mercedes as a rookie for the 2026 season, stepping into one of F1's most prestigious seats. Rookies are rarely expected to contend for wins, let alone the championship, in their first year — the jump from junior categories to F1 typically takes a season or two to fully adjust to. Antonelli has defied that pattern, developing quickly enough to lead the championship standings at the summer break, drawing comparisons to some of the sport's fastest-adapting young stars. **Toto Wolff**, Mercedes' team principal, has closely overseen Antonelli's development since signing him as a junior driver years before his F1 debut.

stories.title: Oliver Bearman turns down Aston Martin, commits to Ferrari's academy through 2028
stories.what_happened: Bearman has turned down interest from **Aston Martin** and is set to extend his existing deal with the **Ferrari Driver Academy** through **2028**, staying at Haas for the 2027 season rather than switching manufacturers, according to reports from motorsport journalist Marc Limacher and other outlets. Speaking about his future, Bearman said he remains "very much committed to what Ferrari have offered me," crediting the team's support since he joined their junior program in Formula 3. The decision comes even though his direct route to a Ferrari race seat has been complicated by **Lewis Hamilton's** stronger 2026 form alongside Leclerc, which leaves both Ferrari seats effectively spoken for. Aston Martin's reported interest in Bearman was tied to uncertainty over 45-year-old **Fernando Alonso's** long-term future with the team.
key_points: **Oliver Bearman** has rejected an approach from **Aston Martin** and will extend his **Ferrari Driver Academy** contract through **2028**.
The 21-year-old Briton is set to continue racing for **Haas** in 2027 rather than switch teams.
Bearman's path to an actual **Ferrari race seat** has narrowed since **Lewis Hamilton's** resurgent form at Maranello.
Bearman said: **"I'm very much committed to what Ferrari have offered me... I'm only sitting here thanks to them."**
The decision ends speculation Aston Martin was preparing a seat for him as a **Fernando Alonso replacement**.

depth.background: **Oliver Bearman** is one of Ferrari's most highly rated young drivers, promoted to a full-time Haas race seat after impressing as a stand-in during the 2024 season. He remains part of the **Ferrari Driver Academy**, the program Ferrari uses to develop and retain young talent it hopes to eventually promote to its own race team. That path has gotten harder this year: **Lewis Hamilton's** improved form at Ferrari, alongside Charles Leclerc, means both current Ferrari seats look locked in for now, leaving Bearman without a clear route to Maranello. **Aston Martin**, meanwhile, has been trying to build a stronger lineup and was reportedly weighing Bearman as a possible replacement for 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

thread.changed: Bearman has now made his choice: he's turned down Aston Martin and re-committed to the Ferrari Driver Academy through 2028, staying at Haas for 2027 instead of jumping ship.
