It's Trump's **second attempt** — the Supreme Court rejected his first try in **June 2026**, upholding broad birthright citizenship.

depth.background: The **14th Amendment** to the US Constitution has long been read to guarantee citizenship to almost anyone born on US soil, regardless of their parents' immigration status — a principle called birthright citizenship. Trump has tried to narrow this since his first term, arguing the amendment wasn't meant to cover children of undocumented or temporary immigrants. In **June 2026, the Supreme Court rejected** his most sweeping earlier attempt and reaffirmed the broad reading of the amendment. Thursday's orders are a narrower, second attempt aimed specifically at 'birth tourism' and a few defined categories rather than undocumented immigrants generally.

stories.title: Houthi missile and drone barrage kills dozens of Yemeni government troops in worst attack since 2022
stories.what_happened: On Thursday, Houthi forces launched a coordinated barrage of missiles and explosive drones at military camps held by Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government in the Marib and Hadramout governorates. Medical and military sources said **at least 30 soldiers were killed**, while Houthi officials claimed a toll as high as **58** — either figure would make it the deadliest single strike on government forces since the 2022 truce. Dozens more were wounded. Spillover projectiles also struck Saudi Arabia's southern Najran region, wounding 11 civilians including seven Saudis, a Yemeni, two Egyptians and a Pakistani national. Houthi military spokesman **Yahya Saree** said the attack was retaliation for what he called a Saudi-backed military buildup near Houthi-held territory. Yemen's government has not yet announced a military response, but the scale of casualties raises pressure on it and its Gulf backers to act.
key_points: Houthi missiles and drones struck army camps in **Marib and Hadramout**, killing **at least 30 government soldiers** — Yemeni officials say the toll could be as high as **58**.
It's the **deadliest attack on Saudi-backed Yemeni forces since 2022**, when a UN-brokered truce froze the front lines.
Stray fire also **wounded 11 civilians** in Saudi Arabia's Najran region, including Saudi, Yemeni, Egyptian and Pakistani nationals.
Houthi spokesman **Yahya Saree** said the strikes were retaliation for a Saudi-backed military buildup near their lines.
The 2022 truce technically expired years ago but **had held informally** — this is the sharpest break from it yet.

depth.background: Yemen's civil war has pitted the Iran-aligned Houthi movement, which controls the capital Sanaa and the north, against Saudi Arabia's **coalition-backed internationally recognized government**, since 2014. A **UN-negotiated truce in 2022** froze the front lines and mostly held even after its formal expiry, even as the Houthis kept attacking Red Sea shipping over the Gaza war. Marib and Hadramout are oil- and gas-producing regions the government controls, making them prized military targets. The Houthis have used long-range missiles and explosive drones — some allegedly Iran-supplied — to strike far from the front line before, including inside Saudi Arabia.

stories.title: US slaps a 15% tariff and a price floor on Chinese-dominated polysilicon
stories.what_happened: On **August 6**, the Trump administration announced it will impose a **15% tariff** on polysilicon and derivative products like wafers and solar cells, alongside new **minimum import prices** meant to stop underpriced Chinese material from undercutting US producers. Both measures take effect in **120 days**, around **December 4**. The action follows a **Section 232 investigation** opened in July 2025 into whether US reliance on foreign — overwhelmingly Chinese — polysilicon poses a national-security risk. Officials framed the move as protecting the remaining US polysilicon factories and rebuilding a domestic supply chain that has all but disappeared: the US share of global production capacity fell from **50% in 2005** to **under 2% in 2024**.
key_points: The Trump administration will impose a **15% tariff** on polysilicon and products made from it, effective in **120 days** (around December 4).
It's also setting **minimum import prices** for polysilicon, wafers, and solar cells — a floor, not just a tax.
**Polysilicon** is the core raw material in both **solar panels** and **semiconductor chips**.
The US share of global polysilicon production has collapsed from **50% in 2005** to under **2% in 2024**, almost all of it moving to China.
The move follows a **Section 232 national-security probe** launched in July 2025.

depth.background: **Polysilicon** is ultra-purified silicon, the base ingredient sliced into wafers for both **solar panels** and **computer chips** — without it, neither industry exists. Two decades ago the US made half the world's polysilicon; heavy Chinese state investment and cheaper power shifted production to China, and US capacity shrank to a sliver. Washington has spent the past year investigating that shift under **Section 232**, the same national-security trade law used for earlier steel and aluminum tariffs.

stories.title: FDA approves Moderna's mFlusiva, the first mRNA-based flu vaccine
stories.what_happened: On **August 6**, the FDA approved Moderna's **mFlusiva**, the first mRNA-based flu vaccine cleared for use in the United States. The approval covers two age groups: a standard approval for adults **50 to 64**, and an **accelerated approval** for adults **65 and older** — the accelerated track is conditional on Moderna completing an additional clinical trial in that older group to confirm the benefit holds up. In a late-stage trial, mFlusiva was found to be roughly **27% more effective** at preventing flu than a standard egg-based flu shot. Because mRNA vaccines don't require growing live virus in eggs, Moderna says it can design and manufacture a new batch in about **six weeks** instead of the usual six months. Moderna expects mFlusiva to be available to eligible Americans in time for the **2026–2027 flu season**, which typically peaks between December and February.
key_points: The **FDA approved mFlusiva**, Moderna's first-ever **mRNA flu vaccine**, on **August 6**.
It's cleared for adults **50–64** under standard approval, and **65+** under a conditional **accelerated approval**.
In late-stage trials it was about **27% more effective** than a standard flu shot.
mRNA tech cuts vaccine development time from **six months to six weeks** — no need to grow live virus in eggs.
Moderna expects it on shelves in time for the **2026–2027 flu season**.

depth.background: Flu vaccines have been made almost the same way for 80 years: grow the actual influenza virus inside millions of fertilized chicken eggs, inactivate it, then purify it into a shot — a process that takes about **six months** and forces manufacturers to guess, months ahead of time, which strains will be circulating that winter. **mRNA vaccines**, proven at global scale during COVID-19, skip that entirely: they inject a short genetic instruction that tells your own cells to briefly manufacture a piece of the target virus, training your immune system without ever using a live pathogen. Moderna has spent years trying to bring that same platform to the seasonal flu shot, and mFlusiva is the first one to clear the FDA's bar.

stories.title: ISI Bill 2026 sparks autonomy fight as faculty warn of central control over India's top statistics institute
stories.what_happened: The government introduced the **Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026** in the **Lok Sabha on August 3**, proposing to repeal the institute's founding **1959 Act**. In place of the current society-based system, the bill creates a **Board of Governors** and a separate **Academic Council**, with governance authority shifting toward centrally appointed members. It also formally widens ISI's academic mandate to include **data science, computer science, cryptology and biostatistics**, and gives it powers to open new campuses and incubate startups. Senior ISI faculty have objected publicly, arguing the bill was drafted without real consultation and would hand control to a **centrally controlled board** at the expense of elected representatives. Opposition leaders have urged Parliament to reject the bill or send it to a **Parliamentary Standing Committee** for closer scrutiny.
key_points: The government introduced the **Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026** in the **Lok Sabha** on August 3.
It **repeals the 1959 Act** and replaces ISI's elected, society-based governance with a **centrally appointed Board of Governors**.
The bill also **broadens ISI's scope** to cover data science, computer science, cryptology and biostatistics.
**Faculty and opposition MPs** want it sent to a **Parliamentary Standing Committee** instead of being rushed through.
ISI has run under its own elected council for **95 years**, since its founding in 1931.

depth.background: The **Indian Statistical Institute (ISI)** — with campuses in Kolkata, Delhi and Bengaluru — is one of India's oldest research institutions, founded in 1931 and long run as a **member-governed society** with substantial say for its own faculty and staff over hiring and research direction. That kind of academic self-governance is common at India's top institutes, but the government has increasingly moved such bodies under **centrally appointed boards** — a pattern already seen with recent changes to IIM governance.

stories.title: Iran says it has a Hormuz shipping deal with Oman — but Washington won't accept Iran's price for it
stories.what_happened: Iran's deputy foreign minister said Tehran and Oman have **agreed on the geographical coordinates** of a proposed safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, with the arrangement covering technical details, security, and a **joint coordination center** to manage maritime traffic — routes would run through both Iran's and Oman's territorial waters. But the agreement does not automatically reopen the strait to normal traffic: Iran says it intends to **charge fees** for maritime services along the route and, according to reporting, wants the plan to **restrict passage for US and Israeli-linked ships** specifically. The US has rejected any such restrictions, with the White House saying it won't accept 'impediments' to free navigation. Iran's foreign ministry maintains it is negotiating only with Oman, not the US directly, even as Trump has said Washington and Tehran would resume separate talks and reiterated he wants the 'immediate, complete and total' reopening of the strait.
key_points: Iran's deputy foreign minister said Tehran and Oman have **agreed on the coordinates** of a safe shipping route through the **Strait of Hormuz**.
The deal would set up a **joint coordination center** with Oman to manage traffic, with routes running through both countries' waters.
Iran wants to **collect fees** from ships using the new route and reportedly wants to **restrict access for US and Israeli vessels** — both of which the US rejects.
The agreement alone does **not reopen the strait** — Washington says Iran must still meet unspecified US conditions first.
This builds on Wednesday's earlier signal that a deal was in its 'final stage,' but the core dispute over who controls navigation is still unresolved.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments pass through — it's one of the most important chokepoints in global energy trade. Iran has periodically threatened to close or restrict the strait during tensions with the US and Israel, most recently amid the current standoff that has included the threat of renewed American military strikes on Iran. Oman, a neutral Gulf state with good relations with both Iran and the West, has stepped in as the broker trying to negotiate terms both Tehran and Washington can live with.

thread.previously: On Wednesday, Iran said its deal with Oman on a new Hormuz shipping route was nearing completion — the 'final stage' of drafting — while Trump said any eventual deal would need to include 'immediate, complete and total' reopening of the strait and stressed that wasn't guaranteed since navigation-control disputes remained unresolved.
thread.changed: Iran and Oman have now actually agreed on the shipping route's coordinates and a joint coordination center, but Iran's push to charge fees and restrict US/Israeli ship access has drawn a firm US rejection — the deal has a concrete shape now, but the same core dispute over control is still blocking it.

prev_ref.title: Iran and Oman edge toward a Hormuz shipping deal, but Trump warns of new strikes if talks collapse

stories.title: FIFA's Infantino apologizes and gets his board's 'full support' after a $4.2 billion World Cup sell-off blows up
stories.what_happened: FIFA's leadership held a crisis meeting in **Rabat, Morocco** on Wednesday after a fierce backlash forced it to abandon a proposal to sell a **20% stake** in a new commercial-rights vehicle, a deal that would have raised roughly **$4.2 billion** from private investors. In a letter to FIFA's Council and member associations, the organization **apologized for errors**, acknowledging the 'process should have been handled differently' and pledging changes so it 'does not happen again.' FIFA secretary-general Mattias Grafström and the management board members present at the Rabat meeting **reaffirmed their full support** for Infantino remaining president. The apology did not fully quiet the criticism: UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister told Reuters the controversy has brought Infantino's leadership 'to a crisis point,' and opposition has come from multiple football confederations and political figures.
key_points: FIFA president **Gianni Infantino** called a crisis meeting of senior staff in **Rabat, Morocco**, after abandoning a plan to sell a stake in World Cup commercial rights.
The scrapped deal would have sold a **20% stake** in a new commercial-rights entity to private investors for about **$4.2 billion**.
FIFA sent a letter to its Council and member associations **apologizing for errors** and admitting the 'process should have been handled differently.'
FIFA's secretary-general and management board **reaffirmed full support** for Infantino, even as a UEFA vice-president called the episode a 'crisis point' for his leadership.
The World Cup is FIFA's single biggest source of income, so how its commercial rights are sold affects funding for football worldwide, not just the tournament itself.

depth.background: **FIFA** is world football's global governing body — it runs the men's and women's World Cups and redistributes the billions those tournaments generate to national football associations everywhere, including the funding that trickles down to grassroots football. **Gianni Infantino** has been FIFA president since 2016 and has increasingly centralized power and cultivated close ties with political leaders, including a widely-noted closeness to Donald Trump during the 2026 World Cup buildup. FIFA had quietly worked up a plan to sell a slice of its future World Cup commercial income to outside investors — similar to how sports leagues have sold stakes in themselves to private equity in recent years — to raise cash upfront.

stories.title: A Russian attack drone crashes in Moldova, deepening fears the Ukraine war is spilling over its borders
stories.what_happened: Moldovan police discovered wreckage from a Russian Geran-2 drone near the village of Văleni in the country's southern Cahul district, close to the Ukrainian border. After examining the debris's construction, materials and identifying markings, specialists concluded it was a Geran-2, effectively Russia's copy of Iran's Shahed-136 loitering munition. No one was hurt. Moldova's foreign ministry condemned the incident as a violation of its airspace and territorial integrity, and authorities have launched a forensic investigation into how the drone entered Moldovan territory. It adds to a string of similar incidents where drones or missile debris linked to the Russia-Ukraine war have landed outside Ukraine, in Moldova, Poland and Romania.
key_points: Debris from a Russian **Geran-2** attack drone was found near the village of **Văleni**, in Moldova's Cahul district.
The site is close to the Ukrainian border; **no injuries** were reported.
Specialists identified the wreckage by its construction, materials and markings as a Geran-2 — Russia's version of Iran's Shahed drone.
Moldova's foreign ministry condemned the **airspace violation** and opened a forensic investigation.
It's part of a **growing pattern** of Russian drones straying beyond Ukraine's borders during the war.

depth.background: Moldova is not a NATO member, but it borders Ukraine directly and has leaned increasingly toward the EU, making it a frequent bystander to spillover from Russia's war — stray drones, downed missile fragments, and airspace violations have happened before, including one incident earlier this year where Moldova said a crashed drone was likely Ukrainian in origin but still blamed Russia's aggression for creating the risk in the first place. The Geran-2 is a long-range, explosive-laden drone Russia has mass-produced using an Iranian design, and it fires them at Ukraine in large nightly barrages aimed at cities, energy grids and military targets.

stories.title: Pakistan beat West Indies by 8 wickets to level the Test series, ending a 3-year away-win drought
stories.what_happened: Pakistan beat West Indies by **8 wickets** in the second Test in Port of Spain, leveling the two-match series **1-1** after losing the opener. West Indies were bowled out for **344 and 117**, while Pakistan replied with **387** and chased down the target for the loss of just **2 wickets**. **Abdullah Shafique** anchored Pakistan's first innings with an unbeaten **160**, becoming the first Pakistan batter since **1977** to score more than 150 in a Test innings on West Indian soil, and was named Player of the Match. **Babar Azam** supported with 88, while off-spinner **Sajid Khan** took 4 wickets in each innings to dismantle the West Indies batting twice. Shafique, who had struggled for a recent place in the side, called the innings a comeback that "felt like a debut."
key_points: **Abdullah Shafique** scored an unbeaten **160**, the first Pakistan batter to pass 150 in a Test innings in the West Indies since **1977**.
Pakistan won the 2nd Test by **8 wickets** in Port of Spain, leveling the **2-match series 1-1**.
It's Pakistan's **first away Test win in three years**.
**Sajid Khan** took **4 wickets in each innings** as Pakistan's spinners ran through the West Indies batting.

depth.background: Pakistan's Test team has struggled badly on the road in recent years, with away wins becoming rare even against lower-ranked sides like West Indies. Abdullah Shafique, once a promising young opener, had fallen out of the side and lost his place in recent selections before this tour gave him a route back in. West Indies had won the first Test of this two-match series, putting Pakistan under pressure to respond just to draw the series rather than lose it outright.

stories.title: Bangladesh opens its first Test tour of Australia in 23 years with a warm-up match in Darwin
stories.what_happened: Bangladesh's touring squad began a three-day warm-up match against a Cricket Australia XI at Darwin's Marrara Cricket Ground, the same venue that will host the first official Test starting August 13. The Australia XI, captained by Kurtis Patterson and featuring uncapped batter Sam Konstas, was picked specifically to give the tourists a tough examination on fast, bouncy Top End pitches before the real series begins. The fixture is a 13-a-side match and does not carry first-class status, underlining its purpose as pure preparation rather than a competitive result that counts on paper. The two-Test series continues with a second Test in Mackay starting August 22.
key_points: Bangladesh begins a **three-day warm-up match** against a Cricket Australia XI at Darwin's Marrara Cricket Ground.
It's Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
The Australia XI is captained by **Kurtis Patterson** and includes uncapped batter **Sam Konstas**.
It's a **13-a-side** fixture without first-class status, aimed purely at helping Bangladesh adjust to fast, bouncy Australian pitches.
The first official Test starts **August 13** at the same Darwin ground, with a second Test in Mackay from August 22.

depth.background: Bangladesh last played a Test series in Australia in 2003, so this tour is a rare and significant step for a team still building its experience in the format's toughest conditions. The visit is part of the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) 2025-27 cycle, where results carry ranking points toward a spot in the eventual WTC final. Bangladesh's squad, led by captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, includes uncapped fast bowler Musfik Hasan, while regulars Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Taskin Ahmed return after being rested for a recent series against Zimbabwe.

stories.title: Cabinet clears ₹84,084 crore 'Samudra Manthan' scheme to ramp up offshore oil and gas drilling
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet approved the Samudra Manthan scheme, a Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas initiative with an outlay of **₹84,084 crore**, running through FY31. It will fund high-quality seismic data acquisition, accelerate deepwater and ultra-deepwater drilling, support scientific drilling in unexplored 'frontier' basins, and build shared offshore production and pipeline infrastructure so discoveries can be commercialised faster. A dedicated **₹2,000 crore** is set aside to build domestic manufacturing capacity for offshore drilling equipment. The scheme targets India's most promising offshore zones — the **Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery and Mahanadi basins and the Andaman Sea** — and is projected to add more than **600 million tonnes of oil-equivalent** in reserves over time.
key_points: The Cabinet approved **Samudra Manthan**, a National Offshore Exploration Scheme with an outlay of **₹84,084 crore (~$8.8 billion)** through FY31.
It funds large-scale **seismic surveys**, **deepwater and ultra-deepwater drilling**, and shared offshore pipeline infrastructure to speed up commercialising discoveries.
**₹10,000 crore** is earmarked for shared offshore production/pipeline infrastructure and **₹2,000 crore** for domestic offshore-equipment manufacturing under Make in India.
Target basins include **Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Mahanadi and the Andaman Sea**, where a single deepwater well can cost **$125-150 million**.
The government expects it to unlock over **600 million tonnes of oil-equivalent** in reserves and cut India's heavy dependence on imported crude.

depth.background: India imports more than **85% of the crude oil** it consumes, a persistent drag on the trade balance and a strategic vulnerability whenever Middle East tensions — like the current Iran-Israel-US standoff — threaten shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz. India's offshore basins are believed to hold large untapped reserves, but deepwater and ultra-deepwater exploration is extremely capital-intensive and risky, which has kept private investment low relative to the geology's promise.

stories.title: Cabinet approves ₹23,731 crore GOBARdhan scheme to turn cow dung and farm waste into clean fuel
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by PM **Narendra Modi**, approved the GOBARdhan National Circular Bioenergy Scheme with an outlay of **₹23,731 crore**, running from **FY2026-27 through FY2035-36**. The scheme will fund infrastructure to convert cattle dung, crop residue, municipal solid waste and press mud into compressed biogas and bio-fertiliser, giving farmers and municipalities a new revenue stream while displacing fossil-fuel and chemical-fertiliser use. It was approved alongside three other major schemes in the same Cabinet meeting — a **₹3.15 lakh crore extension of PM-KISAN**, the **₹84,084 crore Samudra Manthan** offshore exploration scheme, and a **₹36,441 crore Khelo India** revamp — together totalling more than **₹4 lakh crore** in new commitments.
key_points: The Union Cabinet approved **GOBARdhan**, India's National Circular Bioenergy Scheme, with a total outlay of **₹23,731 crore**.
It runs from **FY2026-27 to FY2035-36**, converting **cattle dung, agricultural residue, municipal organic waste and press mud** into compressed biogas and organic manure.
GOBARdhan stands for Galvanizing Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan, unifying several earlier biogas schemes into **one national push**.
It's aimed at boosting rural income, cutting reliance on **imported fuel and chemical fertiliser**, and reducing the crop-residue burning that fuels air pollution.
It came from the same Cabinet meeting that also approved an **₹84,084 crore offshore oil scheme** and a revamped **₹36,441 crore Khelo India** — over **₹4 lakh crore** combined.

depth.background: India has run smaller biogas and organic-waste schemes for years, but they've been fragmented across ministries and states, limiting their scale. Compressed biogas (CBG) — a cleaner substitute for diesel and LPG made by processing organic waste — has been a government priority as India tries to cut its oil and gas import bill (it imports over **85% of its crude oil**) while giving farmers a way to earn from waste that's often just burned, worsening winter air pollution in North India. GOBARdhan consolidates these efforts into one unified, better-funded national scheme.

stories.title: Centre sends a national outbreak-response team to Gujarat and Rajasthan as Chandipura virus kills 22 children
stories.what_happened: Gujarat's health minister confirmed **35 laboratory-confirmed Chandipura virus cases** out of 184 suspected patients tested statewide, with **22 deaths**, almost all of them children under 15. Rajasthan has now confirmed **3 cases** from its border districts of Dungarpur and Sirohi, showing the outbreak is not contained to Gujarat alone. In response, the Union Health Ministry deployed a **National Joint Outbreak Response Team (NJORT)** — a multidisciplinary group of experts from the NCDC, ICMR, and the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying — to both states to intensify surveillance, investigate the source, and strengthen vector-control measures (killing off the insects that spread the virus). The team's job is to submit findings and recommendations back to the Health Ministry on clinical management and public health measures. Investigators are also examining whether carriers beyond the known sandfly vector — including mosquitoes, ticks, and mites — may be involved, which would change how containment efforts are targeted.
key_points: Gujarat has confirmed **35 Chandipura virus cases** out of 184 suspected patients tested, with **22 deaths**, almost all children under 15.
Rajasthan has confirmed **3 cases** from border districts Dungarpur and Sirohi, showing the outbreak is spreading beyond Gujarat.
The Centre deployed a **National Joint Outbreak Response Team (NJORT)** — experts from NCDC, ICMR, and animal husbandry agencies — to both states.
The virus can rapidly cause **Acute Encephalitis Syndrome (AES)**, a dangerous brain inflammation, which is why child deaths have been so fast and severe.
Sandflies are the known carrier, but investigators are also checking whether **mosquitoes, ticks, or mites** play a role in spreading it.

depth.background: **Chandipura virus** is a rare but severe virus, first identified in India in 1965, that mainly strikes children and can progress within days from fever to fatal brain inflammation. It tends to flare up in monsoon season in parts of western and central India, particularly Gujarat, and past outbreaks (including a serious one in 2024) have proven hard to contain quickly because the disease moves so fast and diagnosis can be delayed. India's health system has a standing rapid-response mechanism — NJORT — that brings together the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and animal-health specialists (since insect and animal vectors are often involved) to investigate and contain fast-moving outbreaks like this one.

stories.title: Google's $15 billion Visakhapatnam AI data centre runs into a water and wildlife backlash, with kids marching behind 'We cannot drink DATA' banners
stories.what_happened: Google's data-centre hub under construction in Visakhapatnam, backed by roughly $15 billion in investment and built in partnership with Indian billionaire Gautam Adani's conglomerate, is facing organised opposition from local environmentalists and residents. The core complaint is water: Visakhapatnam currently receives about 410 million litres of water a day against a demand of 480 million litres, meaning the city already rations supply, and activists argue a data centre's cooling needs will deepen that shortage by diverting a public resource toward servers instead of homes. Separately, public interest litigation has been filed over the project's proximity — just 860 metres — to the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary, home to leopards and pangolins, raising concerns that heavy construction and ongoing noise will disturb the protected habitat. In response, Google says it will use "advanced air cooling" technology specifically designed to protect local water resources rather than relying on water-intensive cooling systems. Protesters, including children, have marched through the city holding banners reading "We cannot drink DATA," while supporters of the project point to estimates of up to 188,000 jobs it could create.
key_points: Google is building a **$15 billion** AI data-centre hub in Visakhapatnam, partnered with Gautam **Adani's group**, expected to create up to **188,000 jobs**.
The city already **rations water** — it gets about **410 million litres a day** against demand of **480 million** — before the data centre even opens.
Legal challenges cite the project's construction and noise sitting just **860 metres** from the **Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary**, home to leopards and pangolins.
Google says it will use **advanced air cooling** to protect local water resources instead of conventional water-hungry cooling.
Activists and children have staged marches in Visakhapatnam holding signs reading **"We cannot drink DATA."**

depth.background: AI data centres are enormous physical infrastructure — rows of servers running around the clock that generate huge amounts of heat, which is traditionally cooled using large volumes of water. As global tech giants race to build out AI capacity, India has become a magnet for these projects because of its cheap power, land, and growing digital economy; Visakhapatnam (also called Vizag), a coastal city in Andhra Pradesh, was picked partly for its port access and existing tech investment. But the same qualities that make a city attractive for a data centre — dense population, existing infrastructure strain — often mean water and land are already stretched thin for residents.

stories.title: Mehidy Hasan Miraz's century rescues Bangladesh on day one of their Australia warm-up match in Darwin
stories.what_happened: On day one of Bangladesh's tour match against a Cricket Australia XI in Darwin, the visitors collapsed to 105 for 5 before Mehidy Hasan Miraz built an unbeaten century, finishing on 109 not out off 141 balls with 11 fours and 4 sixes, to drag Bangladesh up to a total of 263 all out. Australian off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli was the standout bowler, taking 6 wickets in the innings. In reply, Cricket Australia XI had reached 51 for 2 after 12 overs by the end of the day's play, trailing by 212 runs. The three-day match, running August 6–8, is Bangladesh's final preparation before their full Test series against Australia begins.
key_points: **Mehidy Hasan Miraz** hit an unbeaten century — **109 off 141 balls** — to lift Bangladesh to **263 all out** in their tour match.
Bangladesh had slumped to **105 for 5** before Mehidy's innings turned the match around.
His knock included **11 fours and 4 sixes**, batting against a Cricket Australia XI in Darwin.
Australian off-spinner **Corey Rocchiccioli took 6 wickets** in the innings.
It's a **three-day warm-up match** (August 6–8) ahead of Bangladesh's full Test tour of Australia.

depth.background: Bangladesh are touring Australia for a Test series, and this three-day match in Darwin against a Cricket Australia XI is their tune-up before the real Test matches begin — a chance to adjust to Australian conditions and get batters and bowlers match-fit without the pressure of a result mattering for the series itself. Warm-up matches like this rarely make headlines unless something notable happens, like a standout individual performance.

stories.title: Opposition MPs stage donation-box protests in Parliament over alleged Ram Mandir theft
stories.what_happened: During Parliament's ongoing Monsoon Session, Samajwadi Party MPs escalated their protest by carrying physical donation boxes into the House, accusing the government of failing to properly investigate the alleged theft and of 'deceiving' devotees. Independent MP Rajesh Ranjan performed a satirical skit dressed as a priest, mock-stealing a donation box before being theatrically 'caught' — Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi joined by placing cash into the box. BJP leaders called the protest 'highly condemnable' and accused the SP of politicizing a religious issue. The protests also referenced Home Minister Amit Shah's absence from the House. Outside Parliament, the Samajwadi Party has continued keeping the donation-theft issue in public view.
key_points: **Samajwadi Party MPs** carried donation boxes into Parliament, accusing the BJP of **'deceiving Lord Ram'** over alleged temple-fund embezzlement.
An independent MP staged a **satirical skit** in priestly robes, mock-stealing a donation box — **Rahul Gandhi** joined by placing cash in it.
The core allegation: a former SP MLA claims **₹7–7.5 crore** in Ram Mandir donations were misappropriated.
**Eight people are in custody** after Uttar Pradesh police filed an FIR following a state government probe.
The **Supreme Court** is separately hearing pleas seeking a **CBI-monitored investigation** into the temple trust's finances.

depth.background: The Ram Janmabhoomi temple in Ayodhya, built after decades of religious and legal dispute, is run by the **Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust** and has received massive public donations — reportedly over ₹5,400 crore. Earlier this year, allegations surfaced that a portion of those donations were siphoned off, prompting a Uttar Pradesh Special Investigation Team probe, an FIR naming several individuals, and Supreme Court petitions demanding an independent CBI-monitored investigation. Because the temple is central to the BJP's political identity, the controversy has become a recurring flashpoint between the opposition and the government.

stories.title: Jharkhand's CID arrests 5 more in a spreading JPSC exam-rigging scandal, taking the total to 19
stories.what_happened: Jharkhand's CID arrested five more people in its investigation into irregularities in JPSC's examination process, taking the total number arrested to 19. The latest group includes the computer operator who worked for a former JPSC chairman, L. Khiangte, along with three students. Earlier arrests in the case included Deputy Controller of Examinations Shweta Kumari Gupta and Ramveer Singh, director of the private firm TSR Data Processing, which was involved in handling exam operations. All are booked under multiple sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS, India's new criminal code) and the Jharkhand Competitive Examination (Measures for Prevention and Remedy of Unfair Means in Recruitment) Act, 2023. The SIT is examining digital records, application logs and related documents as the investigation continues.
key_points: Jharkhand's Crime Investigation Department (CID) arrested **5 more people**, bringing total arrests to **19**.
The new arrests include the **computer operator** of a former JPSC chairman and **three students**.
Earlier arrests included the exam body's **Deputy Controller of Examinations** and a private data-processing firm's director.
JPSC's main exam was **postponed in July** after irregularities surfaced in how it was administered.
Suspects are booked under India's new criminal code (**BNS**) and Jharkhand's 2023 anti-cheating law for competitive exams.

depth.background: The Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) is the state body responsible for recruiting civil servants — the exams it runs decide who gets stable, sought-after government jobs in the state. India has a long, troubled history of recruitment-exam scandals (from national medical-entrance leaks to state police exams), which repeatedly shake young job-seekers' trust in the fairness of public hiring. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) has been digging into JPSC's exam process since irregularities forced the postponement of its main exam in July, and the arrests have steadily climbed as investigators trace a chain from officials to a private vendor to candidates.

stories.title: Bombay High Court overturns Tarun Tejpal's acquittal, convicts former Tehelka editor of rape
stories.what_happened: On August 6, the Bombay High Court's bench pronounced its verdict on the Goa government's appeal, setting aside the trial court's 2021 acquittal and convicting Tejpal under IPC sections **376(2)(f) and (k)** — which cover rape by a person in a position of trust or authority — along with sections 354A and 354B covering sexual harassment and assault. The bench will hear separate arguments on sentencing before deciding Tejpal's punishment. The original complaint dates back to a November 7, 2013 incident at the Grand Hyatt in Bambolim, Goa.
key_points: A Bombay High Court bench of Justices **Neela Gokhale** and **Amit Jamsandekar** overturned Tejpal's **2021 acquittal**.
He was convicted under IPC sections **376(2)(f) and (k)**, plus 354A and 354B (sexual harassment and assault).
The case dates to **November 2013**, when a junior Tehelka colleague accused him of assaulting her in a hotel elevator in Goa.
The verdict came on an appeal filed by the **Goa government** back in 2022 against the trial court's acquittal.
The court will hear arguments on **sentencing separately**, so Tejpal's punishment isn't decided yet.

depth.background: Tarun Tejpal co-founded Tehelka, once one of India's most prominent investigative-journalism magazines, known for sting operations exposing corruption. In November 2013, during a Tehelka event at Goa's Grand Hyatt hotel, a junior colleague accused him of sexually assaulting her twice inside a hotel elevator. The case became one of India's highest-profile #MeToo-era prosecutions, but in 2021 a trial court acquitted Tejpal of all charges — a verdict that drew heavy criticism from women's rights groups, who called it dismissive of the complainant's testimony. The Goa government appealed that acquittal to the Bombay High Court in 2022, and the case has taken nearly **13 years** to reach this point.

stories.title: Pakistan Cricket Board bans domestic all-rounder Hamza Nazar for two years over a misleading visa application
stories.what_happened: The PCB announced a **two-year suspension** and a **PKR one million fine** against domestic all-rounder **Hamza Nazar**, after a disciplinary inquiry found he had submitted incomplete, misleading information and withheld material facts during a visa application process that went through the board. A three-member panel examined the evidence, heard Nazar's own account, and gave him a full opportunity to respond before recommending the punishment. The ban bars him from any PCB-sanctioned cricket, domestic or international, for its full duration, effectively sidelining him from competitive cricket in Pakistan until it expires.
key_points: The **PCB** handed domestic cricketer **Hamza Nazar** a **two-year ban** from all cricket activity and a **PKR 1 million fine**.
The ban followed a formal inquiry into a **visa application process routed through the PCB**, where Nazar was found to have given misleading and incomplete information.
A **three-member panel** reviewed the case and heard Nazar's explanation before recommending the penalty to the board.
The suspension covers **all domestic and international cricket** under PCB jurisdiction, effectively ending his competitive career for two years.
The case is part of the PCB's wider push to tighten discipline around **player conduct and administrative integrity**.

depth.background: The Pakistan Cricket Board has increasingly used formal disciplinary panels to handle integrity breaches by domestic players, ranging from on-field conduct to administrative matters like visa and documentation issues. Boards take visa-related misconduct especially seriously because a player's application often carries the board's institutional backing — false information submitted through that channel can create legal and diplomatic problems for the board itself, not just the individual.

stories.title: ICC unveils 12 host venues across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia for the 2027 Men's Cricket World Cup
stories.what_happened: The International Cricket Council announced the **12 host venues** for the 2027 Men's Cricket World Cup at a launch event in Johannesburg. **South Africa** will host across 8 venues — the Wanderers Stadium (Johannesburg), SuperSport Park (Centurion), Newlands (Cape Town), Kingsmead (Durban), St George's Park (Gqeberha), Mangaung Oval (Bloemfontein), Boland Park (Paarl) and Buffalo Park (East London). **Zimbabwe** contributes 3 venues — Harare Sports Club, Queens Sports Club in Bulawayo, and a stadium in Victoria Falls — while **Namibia's** Windhoek ground hosts matches as the tournament's third co-host nation. The event, carrying the theme **'Three Nations, One Heartbeat,'** will feature the world's top **14 teams** and marks the World Cup's first return to the African continent in **24 years**.
key_points: The tournament will be staged across **12 venues in three countries** — **8 in South Africa, 3 in Zimbabwe, 1 in Namibia**.
It's the Cricket World Cup's **first return to Africa in 24 years**, since South Africa, Zimbabwe and Kenya co-hosted in **2003**.
The tournament carries the theme **'Three Nations, One Heartbeat'** and will feature the **top 14 teams** in the world.
Marquee venues include the **Wanderers Stadium** in Johannesburg and **Newlands** in Cape Town.

depth.background: The ICC Men's Cricket World Cup is cricket's premier 50-over tournament, held roughly every four years and rotated among cricket's major nations. It last visited Africa in **2003**, when South Africa, Zimbabwe and Kenya jointly hosted. Since then the tournament has been held in the Indian subcontinent, Australia/New Zealand, and England, reflecting cricket's commercial center of gravity. South Africa in particular has a strong domestic cricket infrastructure and hosting history, while Zimbabwe and Namibia's inclusion signals the ICC spreading hosting duties and investment more broadly across African cricket.

stories.title: McLaren scrutinizes Ferrari's secret Madrid test as Hamilton downplays any track advantage
stories.what_happened: Ferrari ran **Lewis Hamilton** and **Charles Leclerc** at the new Madring circuit during a promotional filming day last month, with mileage capped at **200km** and the drivers barred from using this year's Pirelli race tyres. **McLaren team principal Andrea Stella** said his team was caught off guard, noting they were 'not informed' Ferrari would be running there and suggesting the Scuderia may have picked up a 'little bit of an advantage' in track knowledge — while acknowledging Ferrari stayed within the rules. Hamilton, addressing the scrutiny this week, said the laps offered little real insight: the surface was 'very, very dusty, as you would expect for a new circuit,' with 'no grip' and tyres 'basically just covered in dust the whole time.' Leclerc similarly downplayed the significance of the running. The episode drew added attention after Hamilton also flagged extreme track temperatures — asphalt readings above **73°C** — as a separate concern heading into the race.
key_points: Ferrari sent **Lewis Hamilton** and **Charles Leclerc** to test the new **Madring circuit** in a promotional 'filming day.'
Rivals were capped at **200km** of running and barred from using **2026-spec Pirelli tyres**.
**McLaren boss Andrea Stella** said his team was **'not informed'** of the session and suspects Ferrari gained a 'little bit of an advantage.'
Hamilton says the track was **'very dusty'** with **'no grip,'** downplaying any edge gained.
The **Madrid Grand Prix** joins the 2026 calendar as F1's newest race.

depth.background: Formula 1 teams are allowed limited 'filming days' using promotional running, separate from official pre-season or in-season testing, which is otherwise tightly restricted to keep the championship competitive. Madrid's new **Madring** circuit debuts on the F1 calendar this year, meaning no team has raced there before — track knowledge itself is a real performance advantage on an unfamiliar layout. Ferrari, tied to the race promoter, arranged a session there last month with Hamilton and Leclerc, which other teams only learned about afterward.

stories.title: Cricket South Africa adds a three-match women's T20I series to India's December tour, ahead of the first Women's Champions Trophy
stories.what_happened: Cricket South Africa (CSA) confirmed on August 6 that it has added a three-match T20I series onto the end of the Indian women's team's already-scheduled multi-format tour of South Africa this December. The full tour now runs from December 9 to 30, with the T20I series — including a marquee Boxing Day fixture on December 26 at Willowmoore Park in Benoni — now the final leg. CSA and the BCCI (India's cricket board) framed the addition explicitly as preparation for the inaugural ICC Women's Champions Trophy, which will be played in Sri Lanka in February 2027. It follows India's most recent T20I series in South Africa in April 2026, which India lost 4-1.
key_points: CSA has added a **three-match T20I series** to the Indian women's team's multi-format tour of South Africa in **December 2026**.
The tour now runs **December 9–30**, ending with the newly added T20Is, including a festive **Boxing Day T20I on December 26** in Benoni.
The extra matches are explicit preparation for the inaugural **ICC Women's Champions Trophy**, to be played in Sri Lanka in **February 2027**.
India lost its last T20I series in South Africa **4-1** back in April 2026.

depth.background: The ICC Women's Champions Trophy is a brand-new tournament set to debut in February 2027 in Sri Lanka, giving national boards a strong incentive to schedule extra practice matches for their squads beforehand. India's women's team already toured South Africa once in 2026, in April, as part of preparation for the Women's T20 World Cup, but lost that series 4-1. This December tour was already planned as a multi-format series (covering more than one format, e.g. ODIs and Tests); the newly added T20Is extend it specifically to sharpen the short-format squad.

stories.title: England recalls Ollie Pope and Brydon Carse for the Pakistan Tests, as Jacob Bethell is ruled out injured
stories.what_happened: England named **Dan Lawrence, Ollie Pope, Brydon Carse and Sam Cook** in its Test squad for the first two matches against Pakistan, with the series opening at **Headingley on August 19**. **Jacob Bethell** was ruled out of the three-match series with a right knee injury, and **Jordan Cox** will move up to bat at **No. 3** in his absence. Lawrence returns to the Test side after **two years** away, batting at No. 6, while Pope — who has averaged **56.66** for Surrey this season — comes back for the first time since England's underwhelming Ashes tour. Carse also returns after wrist and elbow injuries kept him out of the start of the domestic summer, and seamer Sam Cook returns after a solitary appearance against Zimbabwe last year.
key_points: England named its Test squad for the first two matches against **Pakistan**, starting **August 19** at Headingley.
**Jacob Bethell** is ruled out with a **right knee injury**.
**Ollie Pope** and **Brydon Carse** return for the **first time since the Ashes tour**.
**Dan Lawrence** is recalled after **two years** out of the Test side; **Jordan Cox** will bat at **No. 3**.
**Sam Cook** also returns after a one-off appearance against Zimbabwe last summer.

depth.background: England's Test team has been rebuilding under captain **Ben Stokes** and coach Brendon McCullum's aggressive 'Bazball' approach, cycling through batting-order combinations after a difficult **Ashes tour of Australia** earlier this year. **Jacob Bethell**, a young all-rounder seen as key to that rebuild, has been sidelined by injury, forcing selectors to reshuffle the middle order again ahead of a home series against Pakistan.

stories.title: Ferrari junior Rafael Camara plays down talk he'll take Esteban Ocon's Haas seat for 2027
stories.what_happened: Camara addressed the growing speculation linking him to Ocon's Haas seat for 2027, saying he remains fully focused on his Formula 2 title campaign rather than F1 seat negotiations. Recent reporting from Brazilian outlet UOL suggests Haas's plans may have shifted: instead of a race seat, Camara is now expected to sign on as the team's official F1 reserve driver for 2027. That would narrow the actual contest to replace Ocon down to two names — Yuki Tsunoda and Leonardo Fornaroli — while Camara continues developing in F2, where he already has four pole positions and two feature-race victories this rookie season.
key_points: Ferrari academy driver **Rafael Camara**, 21, says he's focused on his **Formula 2 title bid**, despite growing speculation he'll replace **Esteban Ocon** at Haas in 2027.
Ferrari's close ties to Haas make Camara a leading candidate, but reports now suggest he may instead sign as Haas's official **F1 reserve driver** for 2027.
That would leave **Yuki Tsunoda** and **Leonardo Fornaroli** as the main contenders to actually replace Ocon in the race seat.
Camara has taken **four poles and two feature-race wins** in his rookie F2 season as a Ferrari academy member since 2022.

depth.background: Haas has an unusually close technical relationship with Ferrari, using Ferrari engines and gearboxes, which has historically made Ferrari's junior drivers strong candidates for Haas race seats. Esteban Ocon currently drives for Haas, but speculation about his 2027 seat has built as the team weighs its options among Ferrari-linked prospects. Camara is one of Ferrari's most promising young drivers, competing in Formula 2 (the main feeder series just below F1) as part of the Ferrari Driver Academy since 2022.

stories.title: Adrian Newey says Aston Martin's rocky Honda partnership has actually grown stronger after a 'disastrous' start to 2026
stories.what_happened: Newey said the partnership between Aston Martin and Honda has 'progressed' precisely because of, not despite, a difficult start — describing it as fostering an unusually close working relationship between the two organisations as they worked through the problems together. Honda's power unit was unreliable enough early in 2026 that Alonso and Stroll failed to finish the first three races, and a vibration issue in the car raised fears of causing the drivers permanent nerve damage. Aston Martin brought a heavily revised 'B-spec' car to the Hungarian Grand Prix, where the team gained more than a second per lap, and Alonso reached Q2 for the first time all season with both cars recovering positions in the race. The team is now planning to bring an upgraded power unit worth roughly 30 additional horsepower at the Dutch Grand Prix, the first race back after F1's summer break.
key_points: Aston Martin's design chief **Adrian Newey** says the team's relationship with new engine partner **Honda** has strengthened despite early failures.
Honda's power unit caused **three straight race retirements** for Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll at the start of 2026, plus a vibration issue that risked **nerve damage**.
Aston Martin's revised 'B-spec' car gained **over a second per lap** at the Hungarian Grand Prix, where Alonso reached Q2 for the first time this season.
An **upgraded power unit** with roughly **30 extra horsepower** is planned for the Dutch Grand Prix after the summer break.

depth.background: Honda began supplying Aston Martin's power units at the start of the 2026 F1 season, a major new partnership after Honda's long, successful run with Red Bull. New F1 technical regulations for 2026 significantly increased the role of hybrid electrical power in these engines, making the switch to a new manufacturer especially risky. Aston Martin's start to the partnership was rough enough that reliability and safety concerns — including fears of driver nerve damage from a vibration issue — dominated the opening rounds, but the shared struggle to fix those problems has reportedly brought Honda's and Aston Martin's engineering teams closer together.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll climbs to 95 as flash floods swamp 14 districts
stories.what_happened: Assam's flood situation worsened again on Wednesday, August 5, with the state's 2026 death toll rising to **95** after six more people died. The number affected climbed to roughly **1.6 lakh** across **14 districts**, with Sivasagar the hardest-hit (over 57,000 affected), followed by Golaghat (34,000) and Jorhat (25,000). Two people drowned in each of Sivasagar and Biswanath districts, and one person each died in Golaghat and Morigaon. Rivers including the Brahmaputra, Dikhow, Desang, and Dhansiri have flowed above the danger mark in different parts of the state, with some water bodies breaching the 'extreme flood' level. Authorities say this year's flooding has been unusually driven by intense, localized cloudbursts triggering flash floods in south-bank tributaries, rather than the more typical pattern of the Brahmaputra itself gradually rising.
key_points: Assam's 2026 flood death toll rose to **95** on Wednesday, after six more deaths were reported in a single day.
Around **1.6 lakh (160,000) people** are now affected across **14 districts**.
**Sivasagar** is worst-hit, with over **57,000 people** affected, followed by Golaghat (34,000) and Jorhat (25,000).
Two people each drowned in **Sivasagar and Biswanath**; one each died in **Golaghat and Morigaon**.
Unlike a typical Assam flood year driven by the Brahmaputra overflowing, 2026's floods have been unusually driven by **flash floods in south-bank tributaries** like the Dikhow and Dhansiri.

depth.background: Assam floods almost every monsoon season (June–September) because the Brahmaputra river and its tributaries swell with rain from the Himalayas and northeast India, regularly displacing hundreds of thousands of people and damaging farmland. What makes 2026 notable is that the floods have been driven less by the Brahmaputra itself and more by sudden, intense flash floods in south-bank tributary rivers after cloudbursts upstream — even in a year when overall rainfall has been below normal in parts of the state. The crisis has been building since late July, when the toll was already around 80 with over 2 lakh people affected.

stories.title: Jaffna Kings reach Lanka Premier League final as Colombo Kaps crush Kandy Royals in Eliminator
stories.what_happened: On August 5 at Colombo's R. Premadasa Stadium, Jaffna Kings beat Galle Gallants by 14 runs in Qualifier 1 to become the first team through to Saturday's final. Jaffna posted **242 for 2**, built on an unbeaten **108 off 55 balls** from Kamil Mishara, who also took two catches to be named Player of the Match; Gallants fell short at 228 for 8 despite contributions from Sam Harper, Charith Asalanka and Dasun Shanaka. Earlier the same day, Colombo Kaps thrashed Kandy Royals by **68 runs** in the Eliminator, posting 203 for 7 built on Ben McDermott's blistering 71 off 39 balls (one four, seven sixes) and a late flurry from James Neesham (42); Royals were bowled out well short despite two wickets apiece from Nuwan Thushara, Zahir Khan and Shaheen Shah Afridi. That win sends Colombo Kaps into Qualifier 2 against Galle Gallants, scheduled for today (August 7), with the winner meeting Jaffna Kings in Saturday's final.
key_points: **Jaffna Kings** beat Galle Gallants by **14 runs** to reach Saturday's final
Kamil Mishara smashed an unbeaten **108 off 55 balls**, named Player of the Match
**Colombo Kaps** thrashed Kandy Royals by **68 runs** in the Eliminator
Ben McDermott hit **71 off 39 balls** with seven sixes for Kaps
Kaps play Galle Gallants **today** for the last spot in the final

depth.background: The **Lanka Premier League (LPL)** is Sri Lanka's marquee T20 franchise tournament, now in its playoff stage after a round-robin group phase. The playoffs use the standard **IPL-style four-team format**: the top two teams get two chances to reach the final via **Qualifier 1**, while third and fourth place get only one shot each through an **Eliminator**, with the Qualifier 1 loser getting a second life in Qualifier 2. This season's city franchises feature overseas stars including Australia's Ben McDermott and New Zealand's James Neesham.

stories.title: Jaffna Kings smash their way into the LPL final, riding Kamil Mishara's century
stories.what_happened: Jaffna Kings beat Galle Gallants in a high-scoring **Qualifier 1** at the R. Premadasa Stadium in Colombo on Wednesday, sending them straight into Saturday's final. Opener **Kamil Mishara** scored a century to anchor the Jaffna innings, with useful fifties from **Khawaja Nafay** and **Towhid Hridoy** pushing the total well beyond what Galle could chase down. In reply, Galle Gallants got starts from **Sam Harper, Charith Asalanka, Chamika Karunaratne** and **Dasun Shanaka**, but couldn't convert them into a match-winning total. The two innings combined for **470 runs**, one of the highest-scoring games of this LPL season. Galle now get a second opportunity to reach the final by winning Qualifier 2 in the coming days.
key_points: **Jaffna Kings** beat **Galle Gallants** in **Qualifier 1** of the Lanka Premier League, booking a direct spot in **Saturday's final**
Opener **Kamil Mishara** scored a **century**, backed by fifties from Khawaja Nafay and Towhid Hridoy
The match produced **470 runs** in total between both innings
Galle's reply, built on contributions from Sam Harper, Charith Asalanka, Chamika Karunaratne and Dasun Shanaka, fell short
Galle Gallants get a **second chance** in Qualifier 2 in a few days to try to reach the final another way

depth.background: The Lanka Premier League is Sri Lanka's franchise T20 competition, and its playoff format rewards the top two teams from the league phase: the winner of Qualifier 1 goes straight to the final, while the loser gets a second life in Qualifier 2. Jaffna Kings, four-time champions, finished top of the table this season without actually beating Galle Gallants in the league phase, making this playoff meeting their first head-to-head win of the campaign.

stories.title: Trump readies a 15% tariff and price floors on polysilicon to squeeze China out of chip and solar supply chains
stories.what_happened: The Trump administration is set to announce a package combining a **15% tariff** on polysilicon derivatives with **price floors** — legally-set minimum prices — on polysilicon, wafers, solar cells, and finished solar modules. The stated goal is to stop Chinese producers from **dumping** (selling below cost to undercut competitors) polysilicon-based products on the US market, protecting the two remaining US producers. Because polysilicon feeds both the semiconductor industry and the solar industry, the policy reaches deeper into commodity markets than most prior trade actions and affects chipmakers and clean-energy installers simultaneously. Analysts at Roth Capital project the price floor alone could add about **$0.10 per watt** to the cost of imported solar cells, translating into $600–$800 of extra cost on a typical home solar installation.
key_points: The Trump administration will impose a **15% tariff** on polysilicon derivatives, aimed squarely at China
It will also set **minimum import prices** on polysilicon, wafers, cells, and solar modules — a price floor, not just a tax
**China makes 93.5%** of the world's polysilicon; the US has only two domestic producers left
Polysilicon is the key raw material for both **computer chips and solar panels**, so the move hits two industries at once
Analysts estimate the price floor could add **$0.10 per watt** to imported solar cells — roughly $600–$800 more per home solar system

depth.background: Polysilicon is the ultra-refined silicon used to make both semiconductor wafers and solar photovoltaic cells — it sits at the base of two of the most strategically important supply chains in the modern economy. Over the past two decades, **Chinese manufacturers have come to dominate global polysilicon production**, driving prices down so far that most Western producers shut down; today the US is left with just two domestic makers, Hemlock Semiconductor in Michigan and Wacker Chemie in Tennessee. The Trump administration has run a series of tariff actions over 2026 aimed at reshoring critical manufacturing, arguing that dependence on Chinese inputs for chips and clean energy is a national-security risk.

stories.title: Lok Sabha passes a bill making digital bank records valid evidence in court, retiring a 135-year-old law
stories.what_happened: The Lok Sabha passed the **Bankers' Books Evidence Bill, 2026** on **August 5**, moved by Finance Minister **Nirmala Sitharaman**, to replace the colonial-era 1891 Act. The new law widens the legal definition of "bankers' books" to explicitly cover **electronic, digital, virtual, cloud, backup and disaster-recovery records**, and says a **certified electronic or digital copy** of such a record is admissible, valid and legally enforceable as evidence in court — without needing to produce a paper original. The bill next goes to the **Rajya Sabha** (the upper house of Parliament) for approval before it can be signed into law.
key_points: The **Bankers' Books Evidence Bill, 2026** passed the Lok Sabha, replacing the **1891-era Bankers' Books Evidence Act**.
It makes **electronic, digital, virtual, cloud, backup and disaster-recovery bank records** legally admissible in court.
Certified **digital copies** can now be used as evidence **without producing the original paper records**.
Finance Minister **Nirmala Sitharaman** moved the bill in the House.
It still needs **Rajya Sabha approval** before becoming law.

depth.background: The **Bankers' Books Evidence Act of 1891** was written for an era when every bank transaction lived on paper ledgers, and it required those physical books (or certified paper copies) to be produced in court as proof. Indian banking has since gone almost entirely digital — core banking systems, cloud backups, and disaster-recovery servers now hold the records that paper ledgers used to. Courts and banks have increasingly run into friction trying to fit modern digital banking into a 135-year-old legal framework built for paper.

stories.title: China slaps sanctions and tighter drone-export curbs on the US, retaliating weeks before a planned Xi-Trump summit
stories.what_happened: China's Ministry of Commerce announced Wednesday afternoon that it is sanctioning six American companies — including a biotech firm and a resource-analytics company — by adding them to its countermeasures list. Simultaneously, it tightened export controls so that any shipment of drones, key drone components, or related technology bound for the US now requires case-by-case government approval, effective immediately. Beijing described the moves as a 'restrained' response to the US import ban on 43 Chinese companies announced the previous week over alleged human-rights abuses against Uyghur and other minority groups.
key_points: China's Commerce Ministry sanctioned **six US entities**, including a biotech and a resource-analytics firm
New rule subjects **drones and their key components** shipped to the US to **case-by-case scrutiny**, effective immediately
Retaliation for Washington's ban on imports from **43 Chinese companies** over alleged Uyghur forced-labor ties
Comes weeks before an expected **Xi-Trump summit** meant to stabilize the relationship

depth.background: The US and China have spent years locked in an on-again, off-again trade and tech war — tariffs, export bans, and blacklists on both sides. In recent weeks the Trump administration escalated with a ban on importing robots and power converters, blacklisted more Chinese firms over alleged forced-labor links, sanctioned Chinese shipping operators accused of moving Iranian fuel, and added two top Chinese civilian universities to a Pentagon blacklist. Both governments still describe the relationship as aiming for **'constructive strategic stability,'** and a leader-to-leader summit between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump is expected in the US next month.

stories.title: Google DeepMind's CEO steps aside and its chief scientist quits — biggest AI leadership shake-up of the year
stories.what_happened: On **Wednesday, August 5, 2026**, Google confirmed that Hassabis is stepping down as CEO of Google DeepMind to become **Executive Chairman and Alphabet's Chief Scientist**, a role in which he'll concentrate on artificial general intelligence (AGI) strategy and continue leading **Isomorphic Labs**, Alphabet's AI drug-discovery spin-off. Koray Kavukcuoglu, previously DeepMind's chief technology officer and Alphabet's chief AI architect, becomes **Senior Vice President of Google DeepMind**, running daily operations and Gemini model development, and will report straight to Sundar Pichai rather than holding a standalone CEO title. In a separate but simultaneous departure, chief scientist **Jeff Dean** is leaving Google entirely — along with senior fellow Sanjay Ghemawat, DeepMind VP Oriol Vinyals, and Google Brain co-founder Quoc Le — to start **Discovery Loop**, an independent public-benefit corporation aimed at automating scientific and engineering research using AI. Google is a founding investor in Discovery Loop, will act as its cloud partner, and will supply compute for its first year, while **Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures** are co-leading its seed funding round. Reporting from Semafor indicates Hassabis had been quietly handing day-to-day Gemini responsibilities to Kavukcuoglu for roughly **a year** before this was made official.
key_points: **Demis Hassabis**, DeepMind's co-founder and 2024 Nobel laureate, is giving up the CEO title after **13 years running the lab**.
He becomes **Executive Chairman and Alphabet's Chief Scientist**, shifting focus to long-term AGI strategy and drug-discovery unit Isomorphic Labs.
**Koray Kavukcuoglu**, DeepMind's CTO, takes over day-to-day operations and now reports directly to Google CEO **Sundar Pichai**.

Separately, **27-year Google veteran Jeff Dean**, the company's chief scientist, is leaving with three senior colleagues to launch an AI-research startup called **Discovery Loop**, with Google as a founding investor.
The move was reportedly **a year in the making**, not a sudden departure, according to people close to Hassabis.

depth.background: Demis Hassabis co-founded **DeepMind** in London in 2010 and sold it to Google in 2014; the lab became famous for AlphaGo and AlphaFold, and Hassabis won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for AlphaFold's protein-structure predictions. In 2023, Google merged DeepMind with its other AI teams (Google Brain) into one unit, Google DeepMind, with Hassabis as CEO overseeing the Gemini model family and Google's overall AI push. **Jeff Dean** is one of Google's most storied engineers, having co-created foundational systems like MapReduce, Bigtable and TensorFlow over 27 years, and had been serving as the combined unit's chief scientist. This reshuffle lands as Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are locked in an expensive race to build the most capable AI models.

stories.title: Pakistan beats West Indies by 8 wickets in Trinidad to level the Test series and end an 8-match away losing streak
stories.what_happened: Pakistan bowled West Indies out for **117** in their second innings just half an hour into the fourth day's play at Queen's Park Oval, spinner **Jomel Warrican** finishing with a match haul of 6 wickets but Pakistan's own spin attack, led by Sajid and Usman, doing the damage in the second innings with 4 wickets apiece. That left Pakistan needing only **75 runs** to win, a target openers Abdullah Shafique and captain Babar Azam chased down without losing another wicket, both finishing unbeaten on **24**. Shafique, who had scored an unbeaten **160** in the first innings, was named Player of the Match. The win is Pakistan's **first Test victory at this venue since 1977** and their first away Test win in three years, and it levels the two-match series 1-1 after their 90-run defeat in the series opener.
key_points: Pakistan chased down a target of **75** to win the 2nd Test at Queen's Park Oval, Port of Spain, by **8 wickets**
It's Pakistan's **first Test win at this ground since 1977**, and their first away Test victory in **three years**
**Abdullah Shafique** was named Player of the Match for an unbeaten **160** in the first innings
West Indies were bowled out for just **117** in their second innings, half an hour into the day's play
The result **levels the two-match series 1-1**, after Pakistan lost the first Test by 90 runs the previous week

depth.background: Pakistan's Test team has struggled overseas for years, arriving in the West Indies on an **eight-match losing streak away from home** and having lost the first Test of this series by 90 runs. **Babar Azam** is in his second stint as Pakistan's Test captain, having taken the job back after it changed hands following past results, and this tour was seen as an early test of whether his side could turn results around outside Pakistan.

stories.title: Asian stocks post their biggest rally in months as hopes of a US-Iran Hormuz deal lift chip and tech shares
stories.what_happened: Asia-Pacific markets **surged on Wednesday**, tracking an overnight rally that pushed the Dow and S&P 500 to fresh records on Wall Street. Japan's **Nikkei 225 rose 3.66%** and South Korea's **Kospi jumped 3.76%**. Technology and chip stocks led the advance: **SoftBank Group surged more than 10%**, chipmaker **SK Hynix climbed 6%**, with **Kioxia, Tokyo Electron and Advantest** also posting strong gains. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.9%, while Taiwan's Taiex climbed over 3%. The moves were driven by investor optimism that the **US and Iran are close to an interim deal** to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, easing oil-supply fears and reducing pressure on global inflation.
key_points: Japan's **Nikkei 225 jumped 3.66%** and South Korea's **Kospi surged 3.76%**, among their sharpest one-day gains this year.
Chip and tech names led the charge: **SoftBank Group soared more than 10%**, and chipmaker **SK Hynix climbed 6%**.
The rally tracked an overnight **Wall Street record high**, driven by hopes of a US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Investors are betting a Hormuz deal would **ease inflation** and reduce pressure on the Federal Reserve to keep rates high.
Falling oil prices on the same optimism cut energy-import costs across Asian economies.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is a narrow shipping lane between Iran and Oman through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes; Iran had effectively closed it earlier this year amid its standoff with the US and Israel, sending oil prices spiking and rattling markets. Since then, every sign of progress toward reopening it has swung stocks and oil prices sharply, because energy costs feed directly into inflation and corporate earnings. Asian markets — especially Japan and South Korea, whose economies lean heavily on **chip and tech exports** — tend to move even more sharply than the US on this news because they're exposed to both oil-import costs and the global tech cycle.

stories.title: SpaceX's AI spending scares investors even as its results beat forecasts — and hands Nvidia a $200 billion opportunity
stories.what_happened: SpaceX reported Q2 2026 earnings showing spending tied to its xAI unit hit **$15.8 billion** for the quarter — about double the prior quarter and well above analyst expectations of **$13.09 billion**. That AI spending made up the bulk of SpaceX's total **$18.4 billion** in quarterly capital expenditure. Even though overall results beat forecasts, SpaceX shares **sank as much as 13.6%** on Wednesday as investors focused on the scale of AI costs and a looming share-lockup expiration that could flood the market with more stock. Separately, Musk announced SpaceX would use **Nvidia** as its exclusive AI chip supplier for Starmind, running on Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin architecture. Nvidia shares rose more than 3% on the news, with one analyst estimating the partnership could add close to **$200 billion** in Nvidia revenue by 2027 as SpaceX adds roughly 6 gigawatts of Nvidia computing power in orbit.
key_points: SpaceX's AI unit xAI spent **$15.8 billion** on capex last quarter, nearly double the prior quarter and above the **$13.09 billion** Wall Street expected.
SpaceX shares still **fell as much as 13.6%** even though the company beat revenue expectations, as investors focused on ballooning AI costs.
SpaceX named **Nvidia** its exclusive AI chip supplier for a new orbital-computing project called **Starmind**, built on Nvidia's Vera Rubin chip architecture.
Analysts estimate the deal could be worth close to **$200 billion in 2027 revenue** for Nvidia, sending Nvidia shares up **over 3%**.
Elon Musk called Nvidia's Vera Rubin architecture **'the best available'** for the space-based AI buildout.

depth.background: SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket and satellite company, is privately held but increasingly discloses financial details because investors trade its shares on private markets and its Starlink satellite-internet business generates real revenue. Musk has been pushing SpaceX and his AI company xAI closer together, with SpaceX now spending heavily on AI infrastructure — including **Starmind**, a project aiming to run AI computation in orbit, where solar power and cooling are theoretically cheaper than on Earth. This fits a broader **'AI capex' race** across nearly every major tech company (Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta) building data-center capacity for AI models — spending investors are growing increasingly nervous about even as AI revenue hasn't caught up yet.

stories.title: Ajit Agarkar's future as India's chief selector is in doubt, with VVS Laxman reportedly the frontrunner to replace him
stories.what_happened: According to multiple Indian cricket outlets citing sources close to the BCCI, **Agarkar's position has come under fresh scrutiny**, with **VVS Laxman** — a former India batter who now heads the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru and already works closely with the India A and Under-19 setups — emerging as the leading candidate to take over as chief selector. The reported trigger was a **controversy over Rohit Sharma's ODI future** that surfaced during India's tour of England: reports emerged mid-series suggesting Rohit, 39, would be dropped from ODIs after the series, prompting **BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia to publicly deny** any such decision had been made, stating Rohit remained a regular member of the ODI side 'as long as he is in the scheme of things.' Reports suggest this clarification came **without Agarkar's involvement**, deepening friction between the board and the chief selector. No official BCCI statement has confirmed a change is happening — the reports describe this as a likely scenario, not a done deal, with a **formal decision expected at the BCCI's Annual General Meeting in September 2026**.
key_points: Multiple Indian outlets report **Ajit Agarkar may not get a further extension** as chairman of India's senior men's selection committee.
Former India batter **VVS Laxman**, currently head of cricket at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, is described as the **frontrunner** to replace him.
The reported friction traces back to a **retirement scare around Rohit Sharma's ODI future** during India's tour of England, which BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia publicly had to deny.
Agarkar's original term ended in **June 2026**; he was given only a **three-month extension** to September.
A final call is expected at the **BCCI's Annual General Meeting in September 2026** — nothing is confirmed yet.

depth.background: Ajit Agarkar, a former India fast bowler, has chaired the senior men's national selection committee since late 2023, a role that involves picking India's Test, ODI and T20I squads alongside the head coach and captain. His original term as chief selector **expired in June 2026**, but the BCCI (India's cricket board) granted him only a short **three-month extension** rather than a full new term — an early sign that his position was not fully secure. Selectors' jobs in Indian cricket are politically sensitive: they sit at the center of decisions about veteran players' futures, and clashes over timing or communication with senior stars have ended selector tenures before.

stories.title: Supreme Court tells authorities 'listening' — not force — is the answer to student protests
stories.what_happened: On **Wednesday, August 5**, a Supreme Court bench of **Chief Justice of India Surya Kant**, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohan heard a plea from a group of **retired Air Force officers** seeking action against the organisers of the July 20 Jantar Mantar protests. Rather than ordering a crackdown, the CJI used the hearing to set a broader tone: **'In a democracy, during such peaceful marches, forces also should exercise restraint... Responding violently would only aggravate the situation.'** He added that **'the most powerful tool is listening'**, urging authorities to first try to understand and counsel agitating students rather than reach for force. The bench **issued notice** on the specific plea and ordered it tagged with the larger pending batch of petitions from the July protests, meaning it will be heard together with related cases rather than decided today. This followed a related order on **August 3**, in which the same court ruled that **states are free to withdraw FIRs (police complaints) filed against student protesters** — signalling a broader judicial lean toward de-escalation over prosecution. The remarks came the same week the issue was also raised in Parliament's Rajya Sabha, where opposition leaders pressed the government to explain its handling of the protests.
key_points: A bench led by **Chief Justice of India Surya Kant** said security forces must show restraint with young protesters.
The court was hearing a plea by **retired Air Force officers** seeking action against organisers of the **July 20 Jantar Mantar march**.
