stories.title: Progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, handing AIPAC its most expensive defeat ever
stories.what_happened: El-Sayed narrowly defeated Congressmember Haley Stevens in Tuesday's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, in what turned into the **most expensive Democratic Senate primary in US history**. AIPAC and affiliated groups spent up to **$46 million** trying to elect Stevens, the largest sum the lobby has ever committed to a single race, but it wasn't enough to overcome El-Sayed's grassroots coalition. El-Sayed's key backers included Senator Bernie Sanders, Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and the United Auto Workers union. He will now face former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers in the general election in November for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. A win in November would make El-Sayed the first Muslim senator in American history.
key_points: El-Sayed beat establishment favorite Haley Stevens by roughly **1 percentage point** in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary.
The pro-Israel lobby group **AIPAC** and its allies spent as much as **$46 million** backing Stevens — the most it has ever spent on one race.
If El-Sayed wins the general election in November, he would become the **first Muslim senator** in US history.
He is backed by **Bernie Sanders**, **Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez**, and the United Auto Workers, and now faces Republican **Mike Rogers** in November.
The seat opened up because Democratic Senator **Gary Peters** is retiring.

depth.background: AIPAC (the American Israel Public Affairs Committee) is the most powerful pro-Israel lobbying group in US politics, and in recent election cycles it has poured tens of millions of dollars into Democratic primaries to defeat candidates critical of Israel's conduct in Gaza. El-Sayed, a Michigan-born physician and former state health official, ran a progressive campaign that criticized US support for Israel's war in Gaza and leaned on grassroots and union support rather than large donors. Michigan has one of the largest Arab-American and Muslim populations of any US state, and the district's politics have been reshaped since 2023 by anger within the Democratic base over the Gaza war.

stories.title: Brazil's central bank cuts rates for a fourth straight meeting, taking the Selic to 14%
stories.what_happened: Brazil's monetary policy committee (Copom) voted unanimously on August 5 to cut the Selic rate by a quarter point to **14.00%**, the fourth consecutive cut since the easing cycle began in March, for a cumulative **100 basis points** of reduction. The bank's statement pointed to a gradual moderation in economic activity and decelerating inflation measures as the justification, while cautioning that price pressures remain above the official target. The decision matched near-unanimous economist forecasts going into the meeting. The bank left its next move open, saying future decisions will depend on incoming data rather than a preset path.
key_points: Brazil's central bank (BCB) cut its benchmark **Selic rate** by **0.25 percentage points to 14.00%** on August 5.
It's the **fourth straight cut**, bringing total easing since March to **100 basis points**.
The vote was **unanimous** and matched what almost every economist surveyed beforehand expected.
The bank says future moves depend on incoming data, as inflation is **decelerating but still above target**.

depth.background: The Selic rate is Brazil's equivalent of the US Federal Reserve's interest rate — the benchmark the central bank uses to cool or stimulate the economy. Brazil had held rates very high to fight stubborn inflation, and this cutting cycle, which began in March, reflects growing confidence that price pressures are finally easing enough to loosen policy without reigniting inflation. Brazil is one of the largest emerging-market economies, so its rate path is closely watched by global investors as a signal for risk appetite across Latin America.

stories.title: RBI to start rolling out plastic currency notes, beginning with ₹10 and ₹20
stories.what_happened: RBI Governor **Sanjay Malhotra**, speaking at the media briefing after this month's Monetary Policy Committee meeting, said polymer-based currency notes are expected to enter circulation from the start of **next financial year**, contingent on ongoing field trials succeeding. The rollout will begin with the **₹10 and ₹20 denominations** — the smallest, most heavily circulated notes, which suffer the most physical wear. The **central government has already approved** RBI's formal proposal to introduce polymer notes, and pilot testing is currently underway to confirm the material holds up under real-world conditions before a nationwide switch.
key_points: RBI Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** announced the central bank aims to put **polymer (plastic) banknotes** into circulation starting **next financial year**, pending successful trials.
The first notes will be low-denomination **₹10 and ₹20** bills — the ones that wear out fastest from heavy daily handling.
The **government has already approved** RBI's proposal to introduce polymer currency, and field trials are underway.
Polymer notes are **more durable** than paper ones, designed to survive years of circulation without tearing or fading.
The announcement came during the **same press briefing** where RBI held interest rates steady, but is a separate initiative about how currency is physically made.

depth.background: Indian banknotes today are made from a cotton-fiber paper blend that wears out relatively quickly, especially at the ₹10 and ₹20 level that changes hands constantly for small transactions. Countries like Australia, the UK, Canada, and Singapore have already switched some or all of their currency to **polymer** — a thin, durable plastic film — because it lasts far longer, resists moisture and dirt better, and is harder to counterfeit. India has studied and piloted polymer notes on and off for over a decade without a full rollout; this is the first time the RBI has attached a concrete near-term timeline and confirmed government sign-off.

stories.title: India publishes draft voter lists for Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka and two other states under a contested roll-cleanup drive
stories.what_happened: The Election Commission released **draft electoral rolls** for **Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Meghalaya and Jharkhand** on **August 5**, the next step in the SIR process that began with door-to-door enrollment forms between **June 30 and July 29**. Voters, political parties, and civil society groups can now file **claims and objections** to the draft list — flagging missing names or wrongful deletions — through **September 4**. The Commission will process those objections through **October 3** and publish the **final, updated electoral roll on October 7**, using **October 1** as the cutoff date for voter eligibility. The exercise deletes duplicate and ineligible entries while adding newly eligible voters, following the same process already completed or underway in states like Bihar and West Bengal earlier in 2026.
key_points: The Election Commission published **draft electoral rolls** for **five states** — Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Meghalaya and Jharkhand — on **August 5**.
The exercise, called a **Special Intensive Revision (SIR)**, aims to delete duplicate or ineligible voters and add new ones.
Voters can file **claims and objections** to the draft list from **August 5 to September 4**.
The **final electoral roll** is due out on **October 7**, with **October 1** as the eligibility cutoff date.
Opposition parties have accused earlier SIR rounds, including in Bihar and West Bengal, of **wrongly deleting genuine voters**.

depth.background: The **Election Commission of India (ECI)** periodically revises voter lists to keep them accurate, but the current nationwide **Special Intensive Revision** launched in mid-2026 is more sweeping than usual — booth-level officers physically visit homes, distribute forms, and re-verify every voter's eligibility from scratch. Earlier SIR rounds this year in states like **Bihar and West Bengal** drew sharp opposition criticism, with parties including the Congress and Trinamool Congress alleging the process was used to strike genuine voters, especially from minority and migrant communities, off the rolls ahead of elections. The ECI maintains the exercise is a routine accuracy check, not a political tool.

stories.title: Seven years after Article 370, Modi touts a 'new chapter' for Kashmir as Omar Abdullah says he still hasn't 'reconciled'
stories.what_happened: On the **seventh anniversary** of the abrogation, Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted that Article 370 and Article 35(A) **'became history'** seven years ago, crediting the change with expanding infrastructure, education, healthcare, business and sports opportunities across J&K and Ladakh, and reaffirming a commitment to **'inclusive development'** for the region. The BJP marked the day with celebratory events, while opposition parties, including the National Conference, observed it as a **'Black Day.'** J&K Chief Minister **Omar Abdullah** wrote on social media that 'seven years, we haven't forgotten, and we haven't reconciled, far less accepted our current circumstances,' pledging his party remains committed to 'reversing all that was done to J-K.' The anniversary this year fell alongside the 125th birth anniversary of Syama Prasad Mookerjee, the BJP's ideological founder, which the government also marked.
key_points: PM Modi marked **seven years** since Jammu & Kashmir's special status was revoked, calling it a **'decisive new chapter.'**
Modi cited gains in **infrastructure, education, healthcare and business** since 2019.
J&K Chief Minister **Omar Abdullah** said his party has **'neither accepted nor reconciled'** with the decision.
The BJP marked the day as a celebration; opposition parties observed it as a **'Black Day.'**
This year's anniversary coincided with the **125th anniversary** of BJP ideological founder Syama Prasad Mookerjee.

depth.background: In August 2019, India's government revoked **Article 370** of the Constitution, which had given Jammu & Kashmir a special semi-autonomous status — including its own constitution and flag — since 1949. The move split the former state into two federally administered territories, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, and was accompanied by a security lockdown and communications blackout that lasted months. It remains one of the most consequential and contested decisions of Modi's decade in power: the BJP frames it as ending decades of separatism and unlocking development, while regional parties like Omar Abdullah's National Conference call it an unconstitutional stripping of the region's autonomy and identity.

stories.title: Zuckerberg apologises to India over deepfakes and child-abuse content, after a parliamentary panel threatened Meta's legal shield
stories.what_happened: Zuckerberg issued an apology to the Indian government on August 5 covering the spread of CSAM, deepfake content, and operational errors on Meta's platforms, after a parliamentary standing committee on Communications and IT — chaired by BJP MP Nishikant Dubey — gave him a three-day deadline to apologise for the temporary removal of a Modi video. That video, in which Modi addressed students about exam paper leaks, was posted July 23 and taken down for five to six hours before being restored. Government sources say authorities explicitly warned Meta that its role in selecting and distributing content could disqualify it from safe-harbour legal protections if regulators conclude it is actively curating content rather than neutrally hosting it. Meta also acknowledged, per government sources, that it had been paid to boost certain types of content on its platforms.
key_points: Meta CEO **Mark Zuckerberg** apologised to the Indian government over the spread of **child sexual abuse material (CSAM)** and deepfake content on its platforms.
The row began after PM **Narendra Modi's** July 23 video on exam paper leaks was **removed from Facebook for 5–6 hours** before being restored.
A parliamentary panel led by BJP MP **Nishikant Dubey** gave Zuckerberg a **three-day ultimatum** to apologise or risk Meta losing its legal immunity.
Officials warned Meta that if it actively curates what content reaches users, it could **lose 'safe harbour' protection** under India's IT Act.

depth.background: 'Safe harbour' is a legal protection under India's IT Act that shields platforms like Facebook and Instagram from liability for content posted by users, as long as they act as neutral hosts rather than active editors. Indian authorities have grown increasingly assertive about holding global tech platforms accountable for CSAM, deepfakes, and content moderation errors, especially when they touch politically sensitive material. The removal of a Modi video — even briefly and apparently by mistake — triggered exactly the kind of scrutiny Meta has been trying to avoid, because it fed into a broader argument that Meta actively decides what content Indians see rather than merely hosting it.

stories.title: India moves a step closer to building its own fighter-jet engine, in a joint deal with France's Safran
stories.what_happened: Safran and GTRE (India's DRDO-run Gas Turbine Research Establishment) formally submitted their joint proposal for a co-developed fighter engine to India's Cabinet Committee on Security, according to reporting on August 5. The engine targets **110–130 kN of thrust** (roughly 120 kN as a baseline, with room to grow to 140 kN), enough to power the AMCA Mk2. CCS approval, expected before **August 15**, would clear the way for Safran and GTRE to begin final contract negotiations and eventually sign a formal cooperation agreement. The most significant detail: India would hold full intellectual property rights to the resulting engine design, something no previous foreign engine partnership has given it.
key_points: France's **Safran** and India's **GTRE** (the DRDO's engine research arm) have submitted their joint fighter-engine proposal to India's **Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS)** for final approval.
Approval is expected **before August 15**, after which the two sides can begin formal contract negotiations.
The engine is being built to power the **AMCA Mark-2**, the stealthier, more advanced version of India's homegrown fifth-generation fighter jet.
It will deliver **110–130 kN of thrust**, with a growth path toward 140 kN — comparable to engines powering top-tier fighters like the F-35.
Crucially, India would own **full intellectual property** over the engine design — a first for the country in advanced jet propulsion.

depth.background: India has never built a fighter-jet engine of its own from scratch — every Indian fighter, including the Tejas, flies on an imported or foreign-licensed engine, most often from the US or Russia. That gap has long been considered the single biggest weakness in India's push for defence self-reliance (what officials call **Atmanirbhar Bharat**), since an engine supplier can effectively hold a country's air force hostage during a crisis by withholding spares or support. The **AMCA** (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft) is India's flagship stealth-fighter program, developed in two versions — the AMCA Mk1, using an existing imported engine, and the more advanced Mk2, which this new Safran-GTRE partnership is meant to power.

stories.title: PB Fintech's profit nearly doubles as more Indians buy insurance online through PolicyBazaar
stories.what_happened: PB Fintech reported its **April–June 2026 (Q1 FY27)** results on **August 5**, showing consolidated net profit of **₹163 crore**, up 92% from ₹85 crore in the same quarter last year. Revenue from operations rose 40% year-on-year to **₹1,888.28 crore**, from ₹1,347.99 crore. Adjusted EBITDA — operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization — advanced 109% to ₹186 crore from ₹89 crore, with the company citing sharply higher insurance premiums sold through its platform during the quarter.
key_points: **PB Fintech**, parent of PolicyBazaar and Paisabazaar, posted **Q1 FY27** (April–June 2026) consolidated net profit of **₹163 crore**, up **92%** year-on-year.
Revenue from operations jumped **40%** to **₹1,888 crore**, driven by rising online insurance premiums.
Adjusted **EBITDA** (a measure of core operating profit) more than doubled, up **109%** to ₹186 crore.
The results reflect a broader shift of Indian insurance-buying from agents and branches to online platforms.

depth.background: PB Fintech runs **PolicyBazaar**, India's largest online insurance marketplace, and **Paisabazaar**, a loan comparison platform. For years the company burned cash to acquire customers before turning consistently profitable only in the last couple of years, so each quarter's results are watched closely as a proxy for how fast India's insurance market is digitizing. The company has increasingly leaned on its own **PolicyBazaar-branded insurance underwriting arm** to boost margins, rather than just earning commissions for referring customers to other insurers.

stories.title: BCCI selectors are reportedly ready to move on from Rohit Sharma in ODIs, eyeing Yashasvi Jaiswal
stories.what_happened: According to multiple reports, BCCI's senior selection committee under chief selector Ajit Agarkar has decided the team will move forward without Rohit Sharma once the ongoing England ODI series concludes. The selectors and head coach Gautam Gambhir reportedly held talks with Sharma last week to communicate their plans, which include handing an extended opportunity to Yashasvi Jaiswal at the top of the order with the 2027 World Cup in mind. Sharma is said to have raised the matter with a few BCCI officials during the series, reportedly unhappy with how the decision was conveyed to him rather than with the decision itself. Reports indicate the selectors have left the exact timing of any retirement announcement to Sharma, and as of now he has not confirmed whether his current match will be his last.
key_points: Reports say BCCI's selection committee, chaired by **Ajit Agarkar**, plans to go on without Rohit Sharma after the ongoing **England ODI series**.
Agarkar and head coach **Gautam Gambhir** reportedly met Sharma to lay out the plan, with an eye on the **2027 ODI World Cup**.
The panel wants to give a long-term opening slot to young batter **Yashasvi Jaiswal**.
Sharma has reportedly not been fully satisfied with how the decision was communicated, and has raised it with BCCI officials.
The exact **timing** of any retirement has been left to Sharma himself — he hasn't confirmed whether the Lord's ODI will be his last.

depth.background: Rohit Sharma has been one of India's most successful white-ball captains, leading the side to the 2024 T20 World Cup title among other honors. He has already stepped away from two of the three international formats: retiring from T20Is in June 2024, hours after that World Cup win, and from Test cricket in May 2025. ODIs are the only format he still plays, and India's selectors are now said to be planning their post-Rohit ODI batting order well ahead of the 2027 World Cup cycle, a common pattern in Indian cricket where such transitions are debated in the media long before any official announcement.

stories.title: RBI holds rates steady at 5.25%, raises its growth forecast even as West Asia risks cloud the outlook
stories.what_happened: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee, meeting for three days from **August 3 to 5** under Governor **Sanjay Malhotra**, voted unanimously to hold the repo rate at **5.25%**, keeping its **"neutral" policy stance** that leaves the door open to move in either direction later. Alongside the linked **Standing Deposit Facility rate (5.00%)** and **Marginal Standing Facility/Bank Rate (5.50%)**, all key rates stay unchanged. The committee simultaneously **raised its FY27 GDP growth projection to 6.7%** from 6.6%, a modestly more upbeat read on the economy, while **cutting its inflation forecast to 5%** from 5.1%, suggesting price pressures are easing. Malhotra pointed to continuing **global uncertainty and volatility linked to the West Asia conflict** as a reason the committee wants to keep flexibility rather than pre-commit to a rate path. The next scheduled decision is **October 5-7, 2026**.
key_points: The RBI's rate-setting committee **unanimously kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%** for a third straight meeting.
It raised its **FY27 GDP growth forecast to 6.7%** (from 6.6%) and **lowered its inflation forecast to 5%** (from 5.1%).
The committee kept its **"neutral" stance**, meaning it's not committing to cut or hike next, just watching the data.
Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** cited global uncertainty from the **West Asia conflict** as a reason for caution.
The next policy decision is due **October 5-7, 2026**.

depth.background: The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** sets the **repo rate** — the interest rate at which it lends short-term money to commercial banks — roughly every two months through its **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)**, a six-member panel. A higher repo rate makes loans costlier across the economy (cooling inflation but also cooling growth); a lower one does the opposite. India has kept rates unchanged through recent meetings after a run of cuts, as the central bank tries to balance a slowing-but-still-solid economy against inflation and global shocks like the Iran-Israel conflict and its effect on oil prices.

stories.title: A Kuki civil body's total shutdown of Manipur's NH-202 highway begins today, after accusing security escorts of letting goods be seized
stories.what_happened: The **Working Committee of Kuki Civil Society Organisations (WCKCSOs)-Ukhrul** enforced a **total shutdown of National Highway 202** starting at midnight on August 5, escalating a **'counter economic blockade'** it had already been running on the highway since **July 26**. The group says the trigger was an incident in which escorted vehicles — including passenger cars — were forcibly stopped near **Shangkai village**, with goods and commodities allegedly seized. The committee had given the state government a **48-hour ultimatum**, running from August 3 to August 5, to guarantee free movement of essential supplies to Kuki-Zo inhabited areas; when that deadline lapsed, the total shutdown took effect. The blockade exempts medical emergencies, passenger vehicles headed to the airport, and security forces, though the group says all such vehicles are still being inspected to prevent commercial goods from passing.
key_points: The **Working Committee of Kuki Civil Society Organisations (WCKCSOs)-Ukhrul** began a **total shutdown of NH-202** from **midnight on August 5**.
It follows an incident where escorted vehicles on the Imphal-Ukhrul road were **stopped and goods allegedly seized** near Shangkai village.
The group had already been running a **'counter economic blockade'** on the highway since **July 26**, demanding safe passage of essential supplies to Kuki-Zo areas.
It's a **separate flashpoint** from the broader Kuki-Manipur government stand-off reported elsewhere this week — this one is specific to **Ukhrul district**.
The blockade **exempts medical emergencies, security forces, and airport-bound travelers**, though all vehicles are still inspected.

depth.background: Manipur has been gripped by an ethnic conflict between the **Meitei** and **Kuki-Zo** communities since 2023, which has repeatedly disrupted the movement of food, fuel, and medicine along the state's key highways. **NH-202** connects the capital Imphal to the hill district of Ukhrul, and passes through villages controlled by different communities, making it a frequent flashpoint whenever one side accuses the other — or the security forces meant to escort convoys — of failing to protect supplies meant for their areas.

stories.title: Jos Buttler becomes T20 cricket's all-time leading run-scorer as Manchester Super Giants end a losing streak
stories.what_happened: Chasing Welsh Fire's total of 155/4, Manchester Super Giants — powered by explosive half-centuries from Tim Seifert and Jos Buttler — raced to 161/1 off just 69 balls to win by 9 wickets. Buttler's innings, which included six sixes, pushed his career T20 run tally past Kieron Pollard's previous all-time record, making him the format's leading run-scorer across all T20 cricket globally. The win also snapped a three-match losing streak for Manchester Super Giants in the 2026 Hundred season.
key_points: **Jos Buttler** passed **Kieron Pollard** to become T20 cricket's **all-time leading run-scorer**.
He smashed **six sixes** in an explosive innings for Manchester Super Giants against Welsh Fire.
Buttler and **Tim Seifert** chased down **156** in just **69 balls**, winning by **9 wickets**.
The win **snapped a 3-match losing streak** for Manchester Super Giants in this year's Hundred.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's fast-format domestic cricket competition, played each August alongside international commitments, and has become a proving ground and record-setting stage for global T20 stars. Jos Buttler, England's white-ball talisman, has built his reputation over more than a decade as one of the format's most destructive hitters; West Indian all-rounder Kieron Pollard had held the all-time T20 run-scoring record from his own long white-ball career.

stories.title: Parliament clears bill to expand the Supreme Court from 34 to 38 judges, after the Chief Justice warned of a 10,000-case backlog
stories.what_happened: Union Law and Justice Minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal** told the Rajya Sabha that the bill originated from a letter Chief Justice of India **Surya Kant** sent to Prime Minister Modi on **May 11**, warning that the Supreme Court's regular case-disposal rate was becoming unsustainable alongside its Constitution Bench workload, and estimating the Court was accumulating a **backlog gap of about 10,000 cases a year**. The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026 — which raises the Court's sanctioned strength from **34 to 38 judges** including the CJI — had already passed the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha's approval this week completed Parliament's sign-off. The bill now returns to the Lok Sabha for a formality and then goes to the President for assent, after which it becomes law and the government can begin filling the four new seats.
key_points: The **Rajya Sabha** passed the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, completing Parliament's approval after the **Lok Sabha** already cleared it.
It raises the Supreme Court's sanctioned strength from **34 to 38 judges**, including the Chief Justice of India.
The push came after **Chief Justice Surya Kant** wrote to PM Modi on **May 11**, warning the Court can't keep up with its caseload.
The CJI estimated the Court is falling behind by roughly **10,000 cases a year**.
The bill now needs only the **President's assent** to become law.

depth.background: India's Supreme Court, like most of the country's judiciary, has struggled for years with a mounting backlog of pending cases, made worse by the Court's practice of setting aside large blocks of judge-time for **Constitution Benches** — special larger panels that decide cases involving major, unsettled questions of law. Every previous expansion of the Court's judge count (it started with just 8 judges in 1950 and has been enlarged several times since) followed the same pattern: a Chief Justice flagging that the existing bench simply can't keep pace, followed by legislation to add seats. This is the latest such expansion.

stories.title: Sheikh Hasina, exiled in India since 2024, says she'll return to Bangladesh in December — despite a death sentence waiting for her
stories.what_happened: Speaking Wednesday via video link at an event hosted by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia, the **78-year-old** Hasina said she intends to return to Bangladesh **this December**, though she said the exact date would be announced "when the time comes." She acknowledged the risk head-on, saying "I may be detained, I may be sent to prison. But fear cannot decide my duty to the people," and added, "I cannot stay away while my beloved countrymen are suffering." She made the announcement despite having been **sentenced to death in absentia** by a Bangladeshi tribunal over the 2024 crackdown. The Indian government quickly moved to put daylight between itself and the event, stating it neither organized nor endorsed the press conference, underscoring how sensitive Hasina's presence on Indian soil has become for New Delhi's relationship with Dhaka.
key_points: Ousted Bangladeshi PM **Sheikh Hasina** announced she plans to return home from exile in **December**, via video link from an event in India.
She faces a **death sentence** in Bangladesh over the deadly crackdown on the 2024 protests that toppled her government.
"**I may be detained, I may be sent to prison. But fear cannot decide my duty to the people**," she said.
India's government **distanced itself**, saying it neither endorsed nor was involved in organizing the announcement.
The move lands amid **already-strained India-Bangladesh ties**, with Dhaka accusing New Delhi of tolerating political activity against it from Indian soil.

depth.background: Hasina ruled Bangladesh for 15 years before a student-led uprising in mid-2024 forced her from power; she fled by helicopter to New Delhi and has lived there since, while Bangladesh's interim government pursued charges against her and her Awami League party over the violent crackdown on those protests, in which hundreds died. India has never formally extradited her, straining relations with Dhaka's new leadership, who see her continued presence in India — and her ability to make political statements from there — as India effectively shielding her. Bangladesh's next general election is looming, and Hasina's Awami League remains banned from contesting it.

stories.title: Viv Richards wades into the Alzarri Joseph-Daren Sammy row, says the coach's "refused selection" claim went too far
stories.what_happened: Joseph opted out of West Indies' two-Test series against Pakistan, saying the decision was about **managing his workload** after a long injury lay-off rather than any reluctance to play for his country. Sammy's public characterization — that Joseph had **"declined selection"** — drew a sharp response from the bowler, who called the framing **"controversial, without context."** Sir Viv Richards then stepped into the dispute, pushing back on Sammy's phrasing directly: **"he (Alzarri) refused selection, and that's pushing it in my opinion, it's pushing it in a very big way."** Richards said the matter could have been resolved quietly between player and coaching staff rather than becoming a public back-and-forth, and called on both men to **rebuild mutual respect**.
key_points: West Indies great **Viv Richards** publicly weighed in on a brewing dispute between fast bowler **Alzarri Joseph** and head coach **Daren Sammy**.
Joseph sat out the **Pakistan Test series**, citing personal/workload reasons after a long injury layoff.
Sammy said Joseph had **"declined selection"** — a characterization Joseph called **"controversial, without context."**
Richards said calling it a refusal is **"pushing it... in a very big way"** and urged the pair to resolve it privately.
Richards suggested the disagreement could have been handled **without going public**.

depth.background: Alzarri Joseph is one of West Indies' senior fast bowlers, but he's been managing a lengthy injury layoff in recent months. West Indies head coach Daren Sammy, a former captain himself, has been outspoken about squad discipline and commitment since taking the coaching role. Sir Vivian Richards, one of the most respected figures in West Indies cricket history, rarely comments publicly on current team matters, which is part of why his intervention here has drawn attention.

stories.title: ICC finally locks in 12 venues for the 2027 Men's Cricket World Cup, returning the tournament to Africa after 24 years
stories.what_happened: The International Cricket Council confirmed the full list of 12 host venues for the **2027 Men's Cricket World Cup**, announced at a ceremony in Johannesburg. **South Africa** will host the bulk of the tournament across 8 venues — Johannesburg, Centurion, Durban, Gqeberha, East London, Cape Town, Paarl and Bloemfontein — while **Zimbabwe** contributes 3 venues (Harare Sports Club, Queens Sports Club in Bulawayo, and the Victoria Falls stadium) and **Namibia** hosts matches at its national ground in Windhoek. The final will be staged at either the **Wanderers** in Johannesburg or **Newlands** in Cape Town, with the exact choice to be confirmed later. The tournament itself is being expanded to **14 teams playing 57 matches** under a new three-stage competition structure designed to keep more teams competitively alive for longer, under the tournament theme **"Three Nations, One Heartbeat."**
key_points: The 2027 Men's Cricket World Cup will be shared across **South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia** — the 50-over event's first return to Africa in **24 years**.
**South Africa hosts 8 venues**, including Johannesburg, Durban, Cape Town and Bloemfontein; **Zimbabwe gets 3** and **Namibia gets 1**.
The final will be played at either the **Wanderers (Johannesburg)** or **Newlands (Cape Town)**.
The tournament expands to **14 teams and 57 matches**, under a revamped **three-stage format**.
It's built around the theme **"Three Nations, One Heartbeat."**

depth.background: The Cricket World Cup — the sport's premier 50-over (ODI) tournament, held every four years — hasn't been staged in Africa since South Africa hosted it in 2003. Since then it's rotated through Asia, Australia/New Zealand and England, and Zimbabwe and Namibia have never hosted World Cup matches at all, despite both being established international sides. The ICC has been under pressure to grow the game beyond its traditional strongholds, and a three-nation African hosting arrangement was seen as a way to both return the tournament to the continent and share the logistical and financial load across smaller cricket boards.

stories.title: Franco Colapinto's camp opens talks with Williams about an early return, as his Alpine seat wobbles
stories.what_happened: Reports this week say Colapinto's camp has reopened talks with **Williams** about bringing him back to the team early, as uncertainty builds around his position at Alpine for 2027. That uncertainty stems largely from Alpine's ongoing pursuit of Fernando Alonso — Alpine executive adviser **Flavio Briatore** has openly told Colapinto to look for another seat if Alonso decides to join, since Alpine would prioritize the Spaniard. Even so, other reporting suggests Alpine still regards Colapinto as the **frontrunner** to retain his 2027 seat over both Alonso and a separately linked Carlos Sainz. Adding to the complexity, Williams' own 2027 driver lineup isn't settled either — both current drivers, Sainz and Alex Albon, are reportedly considering leaving after a difficult 2026 campaign, which is part of why a Colapinto return there is even plausible.
key_points: **Franco Colapinto's** management is talking to **Williams** about an early return to the team he raced for in 2024-25.
He's currently on loan at **Alpine** through a deal meant to run to 2027 — but that future is now shaky.
Alpine adviser **Flavio Briatore** has told Colapinto to **"find another seat"** if Fernando Alonso wants his spot for 2027.
Despite that, Alpine reportedly still sees Colapinto as the **"overwhelming favourite"** to keep his seat.
Williams' own 2027 line-up is unsettled, with both **Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon** possibly leaving after a frustrating 2026.

depth.background: Colapinto burst into F1 in 2024 as a late-season Williams substitute and impressed enough to be signed on loan by Alpine for the 2026 season, in a deal team boss James Vowles said at the time was designed to keep the door open for his eventual return to Williams. Alpine, meanwhile, has been chasing a marquee driver signing for years and has long been linked with two-time champion Fernando Alonso, who is out of contract at Aston Martin at the end of 2026 and is expected to decide his future during the sport's summer break.

stories.title: Explosive-laden drone found near Ukraine-bound ammunition plane shuts down German airport; officials call it a 'new quality' of threat
stories.what_happened: Shortly before midnight on **Tuesday night**, a flying object was spotted near Leipzig/Halle Airport's south runway, prompting both runways to close and several flights, including a passenger plane, to divert. An airport employee then found a drone carrying what was later confirmed to be a **fist-sized explosive device made with Semtex and PETN**, positioned close to a **Ukrainian aircraft carrying military ammunition**. Police bomb-disposal specialists removed the detonator and made the device safe. Separately, **a second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane** that had aborted its landing because the runway was shut, forcing the freighter to divert roughly 200km to Hanover, where it landed with only slight damage. The north runway reopened after about two hours, and the airport returned to normal operations by Wednesday. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called the incident **'a very serious, security-related' event** and said investigators are treating it as a possible **hybrid attack scenario**, adding that a foreign state cannot be ruled out.
key_points: A drone carrying **Semtex and PETN** explosives was found near the south runway at **Leipzig/Halle Airport**
It was discovered close to a **Ukrainian aircraft loaded with military ammunition**
A second drone **collided with a DHL cargo plane**, which diverted **200km to Hanover** with minor damage
Germany's interior minister called it a **'new quality' of danger** and a possible **hybrid attack**
Officials say they **cannot rule out a foreign power** — suspicion is falling on **Russia**

depth.background: Leipzig/Halle is one of Germany's biggest freight hubs and has become an important stop for cargo flights supporting **Ukraine's war effort**, including shipments of military ammunition. Over the past several months, Germany and other European countries have reported a rising wave of mysterious drone sightings near airports, military sites, and other critical infrastructure. German officials increasingly describe this pattern as part of a **hybrid attack** campaign — deniable acts of sabotage, espionage, and disruption — that they suspect Russia is running against countries supporting Ukraine, without it rising to the level of open war.

stories.title: A projectile sinks an Indian cargo ship off Yemen's coast — all 14 crew, including 13 Indians, rescued alive
stories.what_happened: A projectile struck MSV Faize Noore Oliya on Tuesday while it was sailing about **13 nautical miles south of Al Hudaydah**, Yemen, causing it to capsize and sink. Yemen's coast guard rescued **all 14 crew members** — 13 Indian nationals and one Yemeni citizen — and brought them safely ashore at the **Port of Mokha**. Yemen's Saudi-backed government blamed the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group for the strike, though the Houthis have not claimed responsibility or commented publicly. India's Ministry of External Affairs confirmed the rescue and condemned what it called "continuing attacks on commercial shipping" as "deeply worrisome," while Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal directed officials to arrange the crew's welfare and return home. No fatalities or serious injuries were reported.
key_points: **MSV Faize Noore Oliya** capsized after being struck roughly **13 nautical miles off Al Hudaydah**, Yemen
All **14 crew members** — 13 Indian nationals and one Yemeni — were rescued by Yemen's coast guard
Yemen's government blamed **Iran-aligned Houthi rebels**; the Houthis have not claimed responsibility
India's Shipping Minister **Sarbananda Sonowal** called it an 'unprovoked attack' and ordered welfare support for the crew

depth.background: The Red Sea and waters off Yemen have been a danger zone for commercial shipping for over two years, since Iran-backed Houthi rebels began attacking vessels they linked to Israel, the US, or their allies during the Gaza war, forcing many shipping firms to reroute around Africa instead. That conflict has recently run alongside a separate, escalating confrontation between the US/Israel and Iran over the **Strait of Hormuz**, a critical oil chokepoint. MSV Faize Noore Oliya was a mechanised Indian cargo sailing vessel, the kind of small craft that carries goods along the Arabian Sea and Red Sea coast and has been targeted in Houthi attacks before. The vessel and its mostly-Indian crew were sailing through this contested stretch of water when it was hit.

stories.title: West Indies fight back to lead by 60 but slip to 103 for 6 as Pakistan's bowlers seize control of the series-deciding Trinidad Test
stories.what_happened: Pakistan were bowled out for **387** in their first innings, a lead of **43 runs** over West Indies' 344, built on **Abdullah Shafique's unbeaten 160** and a fighting **88 from captain Babar Azam**, who was run out just short of what would have been his first Test century in four years. West Indies then batted again in their second innings and slipped to **103 for 6** by the close of day three, with **Sajid Khan taking 4 for 32** and Ali Usman claiming two more wickets to spark a late-session collapse. That leaves West Indies **60 runs ahead** overall but with only four second-innings wickets standing, putting Pakistan in a strong position to wrap up the match and the series on day four.
key_points: West Indies closed **day three at 103 for 6**, leading Pakistan's first-innings **387** by just **60 runs** with only **4 wickets in hand**.
**Sajid Khan took 4 for 32** in the second innings to trigger the collapse after West Indies looked set to build a big lead.
Pakistan's first innings finished on **387**, built on **Abdullah Shafique's unbeaten 160** and **Babar Azam's 88**.
**Babar Azam was run out for 88**, denying him his first Test century in four years.
A win would give Pakistan their **first away Test victory since 2023** and decide this series.

depth.background: Pakistan and West Indies are locked in a **series-deciding 2nd Test** in Port of Spain, Trinidad, after West Indies won the first Test. West Indies had batted first and posted **344**, before Pakistan's reply — anchored by Abdullah Shafique's marathon innings — pulled them into the lead. With the series on the line, every session has swung the momentum, and Pakistan chasing their first Test win away from home since 2023 raises the stakes further.

stories.title: New Zealand great Suzie Bates returns to Otago domestic cricket for the first time in 20 years

stories.title: AMD posts record $11.5 billion quarter as AI chip demand doubles its data-center revenue — but the stock falls 8%

The star of the report was the data-center segment — servers and AI accelerator chips — where revenue **more than doubled to $6.7 billion**, driven by demand for AMD's EPYC server processors and Instinct AI GPUs. Both revenue and adjusted earnings-per-share ($1.66) beat what Wall Street analysts had forecast. AMD guided for roughly **$13 billion** in revenue next quarter. Even so, the stock dropped **about 8-9%** in after-hours trading, as investors had been positioned for an even larger beat given the stock had already risen sharply heading into the report.
key_points: AMD's revenue hit a **company record of $11.5 billion**, up **50% year-over-year**.
**Data-center revenue more than doubled**, up **107%** to **$6.7 billion** — now **58% of all AMD sales**.

depth.background: AMD makes the chips (CPUs and GPUs) that power servers and AI systems, competing most directly with Nvidia in the booming market for AI data-center hardware. Investors have bid AI-chip stocks up sharply over the past two years on the bet that demand for AI computing power will keep compounding, which means **even a strong quarter can disappoint** if it doesn't beat already-sky-high expectations.

stories.title: Kuki tribal body lifts its Manipur economic blockade — but gives the government a fresh 48-hour ultimatum to deliver food and fuel
stories.what_happened: **Kuki Inpi Manipur (KIM)**, the apex tribal body representing Kuki communities in the state, announced it was lifting its own economic blockade on Kuki-Zo areas 'with immediate effect,' saying the move came 'in good faith' after the state government assured it that adequate food grains, fuel, medicine and other essential commodities would be supplied to the affected regions. Those regions had been reeling under acute shortages during the blockade, with prices for a 50-kg bag of rice reportedly climbing to around ₹4,000 and petrol reaching roughly ₹280 per litre in the worst-hit areas. KIM was explicit that lifting the blockade should not be read as backing down from its underlying demands, and it set the government a fresh 48-hour deadline to turn its assurances into actual deliveries on the ground. The organisation said its patience 'may be short-lived' if the government's promises aren't honoured within that window.
key_points: **Kuki Inpi Manipur (KIM)**, the apex Kuki tribal body, withdrew its economic blockade **'in good faith'** after government assurances.
It has now given the state government a fresh **48-hour deadline** to actually deliver food, fuel and medicine to Kuki-Zo areas.
The blockade had caused severe shortages — a **50-kg bag of rice** reportedly hit **₹4,000** and petrol touched **₹280/litre** in affected areas.
KIM warned the withdrawal is **not a retreat** from its demands, and its patience 'may be short-lived' if relief doesn't arrive.
This is the latest flashpoint in Manipur's long-running **Kuki-Zo vs Meitei** ethnic conflict over land, supply routes and security.

depth.background: Manipur has been gripped by ethnic conflict between the Kuki-Zo and Meitei communities since violence broke out in May 2023, killing hundreds and displacing tens of thousands. Highways and supply routes running through Kuki-Zo areas have repeatedly become flashpoints, with blockades — by both communities, at different times — used as a form of leverage to pressure the state government over security, essential supplies, and political demands. We reported yesterday that a separate Kuki-Zo civil society body in Ukhrul district had given the government a 48-hour deadline over what it called a **selective blockade** of Kuki-Zo supplies, threatening a total shutdown.

stories.title: Trump calls off a planned strike on Iran, saying a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could land 'today or tomorrow' — but Iran denies it's talking to Washington
stories.what_happened: President Trump said Saturday night, August 1, that he had called off a planned attack on Iran because 'the perimeters of a deal had been agreed to' — one that would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping and end Iran's nuclear threat. He said the strike would have been the **'biggest attack since World War II.'** Trump initially said US-Iran negotiations would resume Monday, August 3, but Iran publicly denied this, saying it was not negotiating directly with the US at all and was instead talking only to **Oman** about establishing a temporary, safe shipping route through the strait. Trump responded by calling Iran's leadership 'unbelievably duplicitous' on social media. By Tuesday, August 4, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a deal could be reached **'today or tomorrow,'** while Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed progress in the Oman-mediated track but said there was **'not finality yet.'** Trump has said he faces no time pressure since he isn't seeking re-election.

Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** says an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come **'today or tomorrow.'**

depth.background: Iran and the US have spent months in an escalating standoff that has repeatedly threatened to spill into open war, with Iran's nuclear program and its ability to choke off the **Strait of Hormuz** — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil passes through — at the center of it. Trump had set Iran a 'last chance' deadline to sign a deal or face strikes explicitly aimed at 'decapitating' its leadership. That threat was real enough that Trump says he had a full attack plan ready to go before pulling back at the last minute.

stories.title: Sergio Perez says there's 'no loyalty' in F1, reflecting on being dropped by his old team after saving it from collapse
stories.what_happened: In new comments, Perez discussed his complicated history with the team now known as **Aston Martin**, saying that despite everything he did for the outfit — including helping push it into **administration proceedings** to protect jobs after its former owner, Kingfisher Airlines, collapsed in 2018 — he was ultimately let go. **'I was like, look, there is no loyalty in this sport,'** he said, adding that he didn't take the move personally and instead focused on performing on track. He pointed to winning the **2020 Sakhir Grand Prix** — the team's first win in any guise, and the first for the Force India/Racing Point lineage since Jordan's last win in 2003 — as the highlight that came from that focus. Perez said he maintains a good relationship with people at Aston Martin despite the way things ended.
key_points: Sergio Perez opened up about being **dropped by Racing Point (now Aston Martin)** despite having helped **save the team from administration** years earlier.
He said plainly: **'There is no loyalty in this sport'** — but added he didn't take the dismissal personally.
Perez credited his own **Sakhir Grand Prix win** — the team's **first-ever victory**, and its first since Jordan in 2003 — as a turning point he's proud of.

He traced his history with the outfit back to **2014**, when it was still called **Force India**, and described leading efforts to save it from financial collapse after Kingfisher Airlines' collapse in **2018**.
The comments come as Perez now drives for **Cadillac**, F1's newest team, reflecting on a career that has spanned multiple team identities and ownership changes.

depth.background: Sergio Perez's F1 career has been intertwined with one team through several rebrands: he joined as **Force India** in 2014, stayed on through its financial troubles and rescue in **2018** (when it became Racing Point), delivered the team's breakthrough win at the **2020 Sakhir Grand Prix**, and then watched it transform into **Aston Martin** under new ownership before being dropped. He's now racing for **Cadillac**, F1's brand-new American team that joined the grid this season. His comments reflect a broader truth in Formula 1: team ownership, sponsorship, and driver line-ups change fast, and even drivers who help save a team from extinction aren't guaranteed a long-term seat.

stories.title: A US appeals court says Perplexity's AI shopping bot didn't 'hack' Amazon — because it was the user, not the AI, doing the clicking
stories.what_happened: The Ninth Circuit reversed the injunction, finding Amazon unlikely to succeed in proving Perplexity itself violated the CFAA. The court's reasoning: it's the human user, directing Comet to complete a shopping task with their own Amazon credentials, who "accesses" Amazon's systems — not Perplexity. Perplexity's Comet agent can therefore resume shopping on Amazon on users' behalf immediately. The underlying lawsuit — over whether Perplexity's tool violates Amazon's terms of service or unfairly free-rides on its platform — continues in a San Francisco federal court. Amazon can seek a rehearing before a larger Ninth Circuit panel or ask the **Supreme Court** to take the case.
key_points: The **Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals** overturned a lower-court order banning Perplexity's **Comet AI shopping agent** from Amazon.com.
The court ruled it is **users, not Perplexity**, who 'access' Amazon's computers under federal hacking law — even when an AI agent does the clicking.
Amazon sued in late 2025 alleging Comet **unlawfully accessed password-protected accounts**; a judge granted an injunction in **March 2026**.
The ruling turns on the **Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)**, America's main anti-hacking law, written decades before AI agents existed.
Amazon can still seek a **rehearing or Supreme Court review**; the underlying lawsuit continues in San Francisco.

depth.background: AI "agent" browsers like Perplexity's Comet can log into a user's own accounts and complete tasks — such as buying something on Amazon — on the user's behalf, without the user clicking through each step. Amazon saw this as a threat to how it controls its own site and sued Perplexity in late 2025, arguing the AI agent's automated access was the kind of unauthorized computer access the 1986 **Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)** was written to punish. A federal judge sided with Amazon in March 2026 and blocked Comet from shopping on Amazon while the case played out. Perplexity appealed, arguing that when a user directs their own AI agent to buy something with their own login, it's still fundamentally the user — not Perplexity — accessing the site.

stories.title: Bharti Airtel's profit jumps 37% to ₹8,167 crore as it adds 5 million smartphone users and squeezes more revenue per customer
stories.what_happened: Bharti Airtel reported its first-quarter results for FY27 (April-June 2026) on August 4, posting a consolidated net profit of **₹8,167.4 crore**, up 37.3% from ₹5,947.9 crore in the same quarter last year. Revenue from operations rose 18.35% to ₹58,539.1 crore, from ₹49,462.6 crore a year earlier. The company added 5 million smartphone customers during the quarter, and its average revenue per user (ARPU) climbed to ₹264 — the highest in the Indian telecom industry. The profit figure was affected by two offsetting one-off items: a ₹353.4 crore exceptional charge tied to a provisional settlement of a commercial dispute at one of the group's subsidiaries, and a ₹389.8 crore exceptional tax benefit from a favourable ruling related to an earlier year's business losses. Ahead of the results, brokerages and analysts had broadly expected an even sharper profit jump of around 45% year-on-year.
key_points: Consolidated net profit rose **37.3% year-on-year to ₹8,167.4 crore** for the quarter ended June 30.
Revenue climbed **18.35% to ₹58,539.1 crore**, driven by subscriber growth and pricing power.
**ARPU** (average revenue per user) rose to **₹264**, an industry-leading figure, as Airtel added **5 million** smartphone customers.
Profit was dented by a **₹353.4 crore** exceptional charge for a subsidiary dispute settlement, offset by a **₹389.8 crore** tax benefit from an earlier favourable order.
Analysts had penciled in an even bigger jump of around **45%** — the actual number, while strong, came in below the loftiest estimates.

depth.background: Bharti Airtel is India's second-largest telecom operator by subscribers, competing chiefly with Reliance Jio and Vodafone Idea in a market that has consolidated to three major private players plus state-run BSNL. Since India's telecom price wars ended, operators have focused on **ARPU** growth — charging existing users more, especially by pushing them toward higher-value data and 4G/5G plans — rather than just chasing new subscribers, as the main lever for profit growth.
